title: TSP: the VTC-facing ceremonies still cannot use TSP (the VTA surface now can)
body:
OpenVTC cannot speak TSP, and until #187 it did not even *say* that a VTA offers it.

Against a TSP-enabled VTA
(`did:webvh:QmWoJD2kpP6AJknNtj7UFERUstEen258ywj3ruHoh1ZAqr:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta`),
whose DID document advertises `#tsp` / `TSPTransport` alongside `#vta-didcomm`,
the VTA panel rendered:

```
Transport:  DIDComm  (in use)   ·   only transport offered
```

which was false — TSP is offered.

## 1. Tell the truth about TSP — **DONE** (#187)

`AdvertisedTransports` gained `tsp_mediator_did`, carried from
`ResolvedVta` (vta-sdk 0.20, upstream #765). The panel now renders
`DIDComm (in use) · TSP advertised (not yet supported)`, keeping
advertised-but-unsupported distinct from both "available" and "absent" (R6.4).
The adjacent `REST endpoint …` inconsistency is fixed too — it is labelled
`(configured; not advertised)` only when the probe positively established the
VTA advertises no `#vta-rest`.

## 2. Speak TSP — **re-scoped**

The upstream blockers (#765, #766, #767) are all closed, and vta-sdk 0.20 ships
`VtaClient::connect_tsp` / `Transport::Tsp`. But the original plan for this
section assumed TSP is a drop-in replacement transport, and it is not. What
follows replaces it.

### What the investigation found

**(a) TSP carries the Trust-Task surface only.** `Transport::Tsp` serves
`rpc_tt`. The VTA's TSP inbound dispatcher hands each unpacked payload to
`dispatch_trust_task_core` and has no handler behind the older DIDComm
*protocol-message* surface, so those operations return `UnsupportedTransport`
**by design** (`vta-sdk/src/client/mod.rs:161`, and the `Transport::Tsp` doc at
`:53`).

**(b) Every `VtaClient` operation OpenVTC uses is on the surface TSP does not
carry.** Checked one by one — all `rpc` / `rpc_void`:

| Operation | Call sites | Dispatch |
|---|---|---|
| `get_key_secret` | 13 | `rpc` |
| `create_key` | 7 | `rpc` |
| `create_did_webvh` | 1 | `rpc` |
| `delete_did_webvh` | 1 | `rpc_void` |
| `list_contexts` | 1 | `rpc` |
| `list_webvh_servers` | 1 | `rpc` |

So putting OpenVTC's runtime VTA client on TSP would break key management, DID
minting, and context listing. **This is what invalidates "`build_runtime_vta_client`
becomes a three-way choice" and "add a `VtaTransport::Tsp` variant"** — there is
no single client-wide transport choice that is correct.

**(c) One `VtaClient` surface *can* move today.** `dispatch_trust_task`
implements all three transports (`client/mod.rs:960`), TSP included — same
request/reply document on every one. OpenVTC reaches it from
`agent_name_manage.rs` for the six `did-management/agent-name` Trust Tasks
(set / remove / enable / disable / list / check). That is the whole of the
currently-movable VTA surface.

**(d) The SDK's TSP selection machinery is not on the path OpenVTC uses.**
`TransportChoice` (with `Auto` = TSP > DIDComm > REST, bounded connects via
`TSP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT` / `DIDCOMM_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`, env overrides,
and a deliberately *loud* fallback) lives on
`SessionStore::connect_with_transport` — the `pnm`/`cnm` connect path. OpenVTC
goes through `build_runtime_vta_client` → `VtaClient::connect_auto`, which in
0.20 is still strictly DIDComm-vs-REST with no TSP arm. Either we adopt the
session-store path or we reimplement that policy; **we must not reimplement it
silently**, because the fallback-loudness rationale is the kind of decision the
SDK docs record precisely so consumers don't quietly diverge.

**(e) The messaging layer already supports TSP properly, and this is the bigger
prize.** `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` 0.3.20 — the version already in
our lockfile — has `Protocols { didcomm, tsp }` with `Protocols::BOTH`
multiplexing **both protocols on one websocket per DID** (the mediator allows
only one socket per DID), plus a `TspHandler` trait symmetric with
`DIDCommHandler` and a `TspResponse` the service seals and routes for you. So
per-surface routing at the messaging layer needs **no second mediator session** —
which sidesteps the session-duel and leak hazards this codebase documents at
length. Correlation is explicitly the application's concern: a TSP frame carries
no thread id, so a request/response id has to live in the payload (e.g. a Trust
Task `#response` document's `threadId`).

**(f) The `tsp` feature is cheap.** Enabling it on `vta-sdk` (pulling
`affinidi-tdk/tsp` + `affinidi-messaging-sdk/tsp`) builds clean and costs
**+148,944 bytes on the release binary — +0.82%** (18,112,368 → 18,261,312,
macOS arm64, `lto = true`, `strip = "symbols"`). No reason to make it
conditional.

### Revised work

**2a — Per-surface transport model.** `VtaTransports::in_use` stops being a
single value. A process can be on DIDComm for protocol messages *and* TSP for
trust tasks at the same time, so the panel headline expresses a pair, not a third
enum case. Must stay derivable synchronously from stored config with no network —
the property that lets the panel distinguish "we are on X" from "we could not
ask".

**2b — TSP for the trust-task surface (`dispatch_trust_task`).** Enable the
`tsp` feature; connect TSP *alongside* the DIDComm client rather than instead of
it; route the six `agent_name_manage` operations over it when the VTA advertises
`#tsp`. Protocol-message operations stay on DIDComm — unconditionally, not as a
fallback.

**2c — Transport preference + override.** Persist the operator's choice and
expose an override, so a broken TSP deployment has a documented recovery path to
DIDComm rather than a hang. Mirror `TransportChoice`'s semantics rather than
inventing new ones, including that `Auto`'s fallback is *loud*.

**2d — Bounds and error text.** Every TSP connect and wait bounded (R1.2), with
network-unreachable / not-advertised / auth-rejected carrying distinct text
(R6.4). Reuse the SDK's env-override names where they apply.

**2e — MockVta coverage.** A TSP-advertising VTA in the harness, so the selection
logic has a test that does not need the live deployment.

**2f — Messaging-layer TSP (separate slice, largest).** `Protocols::BOTH` on the
persona listeners plus a `TspHandler` feeding the existing dispatch, for the
VTC-facing ceremonies (join, VIC, credential flows). Blocked on the VTC
advertising `#tsp` and on a correlation decision per (e). Worth its own issue
once 2a–2e land.

## Context

The TSP transport itself is live end-to-end — mediator on
`affinidi-messaging-mediator` 0.17.7, correlated ping, real pongs from the
deployed VTA (#749, #750). The gap was never the wire; it is which surfaces a
client may legitimately move onto it.

title: feat: run the join ceremony over TSP when the community offers it (#201)
body:
feat: run the join ceremony over TSP when the community offers it (#201)

Completes #185. The VTC-facing ceremonies could not use TSP: OpenVTC had no
way to send a Trust Task as a TSP frame, and dropped every inbound one.

Both halves had to land together. The VTC never initiates TSP to a member
(tsp-enablement.md §14 Q4), so inbound routing alone would have been dead
code and outbound alone would have thrown away the reply.

  * Inbound was never a missing transport -- only missing routing.
    `DidCommTransport` owns the one mediator socket and already surfaces TSP
    frames off it, unpacked and sender-authenticated, tagged
    `Protocol::TSP`. The dispatcher discarded them at its first line, which
    was a deliberate placeholder. `tsp_frame_to_message` now normalises a
    frame into the `Message` shape everything downstream speaks.

    That mapping is lossless because both transports carry the SAME
    document: DIDComm's envelope merely repeats `type` and threads on the
    request id, so the normaliser reads those back out of the document.
    `body` is the whole document, which is exactly what `tt_didcomm_reply`
    puts there -- so every existing handler works unchanged. This only holds
    because #200 taught them to unwrap `payload`; before it, every TSP reply
    would have parsed at the wrong nesting.

  * Outbound is one call `pack_and_send` cannot make. It forwards a DIDComm
    `routing/2.0` envelope unconditionally, so `tsp::send_trust_task` is its
    TSP counterpart: same signature shape, `send_routed` with the peer's
    ADVERTISED mediator as the routing hop and the peer as the recipient.

  * Correlation had to be made to agree. DIDComm threads the reply on the
    request MESSAGE id; TSP has no message and threads on the request
    DOCUMENT id. Two different UUIDs -- so the DIDComm message is now built
    with `id` equal to the document id. `Uuid::parse_str` accepts the
    `urn:uuid:` form, so the existing correlation code reads either
    unchanged, and one handle works on both wires.

  * Discovery is per-send and degrades quietly. `peer_tsp_mediator` runs the
    same `#tsp` lookup against the community's document that the VTA path
    already runs; not-advertised, unresolvable and timed-out all mean "use
    DIDComm", with the distinction kept in the log (R6.4). A community that
    has not been flipped is unaffected.

Deliberately NOT a `MessageTransport` on the delivery layer, which an
earlier draft made it. The ceremony sends do not go through that layer at
all, so an outbox-backed TSP leg would have given TSP joins durability
DIDComm joins lack and hidden a reliability change inside a transport
change. Putting the ceremonies behind the outbox is worth doing -- for both
transports, as its own change.

Verified against the live deployment's shapes: the test VTC
(did:webvh:QmXi1PZD4...:webvh.storm.ws:first-vtc) now advertises `#tsp` at
the shared mediator, and the VTC accepts Trust Tasks over TSP as of VTI #833
with the member verbs added in #838.

cargo test --workspace green (290 openvtc-core + 255 openvtc + every
integration binary, 0 failed); six new tests cover the normaliser --
including that a frame with no proven sender does not inherit the document's
`issuer`, which would let any TSP peer claim to be the VTC. fmt, clippy
--all-targets, rustdoc -D warnings and --locked all clean.

Closes #185

title: chore(tee): one home for the TEE store keys, and a changelog guard that can fail
body:
Three small cross-cutting fixes that surfaced while reviewing the TEE / Nitro batch (#819, #824, #826, #827, #832). None of them belongs to any one of those PRs, so they are collected here rather than bolted onto whichever happened to touch the file.

Independent of each other and of the PRs that surfaced them — mergeable in any order.

## 1. `tee:did_log` / `tee:vta_did` get one home

The DID-log store key was a bare string literal in **four** places across three crates:

| Site | Role |
|---|---|
| `vta-tee/src/did_autogen.rs` (×2) | writes it to the `KEYS` (encrypted) and `BOOTSTRAP` (plain) keyspaces |
| `vta-service/src/routes/attestation.rs` | reads it to serve `GET /attestation/did-log` |
| `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/src/storage.rs` (×2) | parent-side reader that writes `did.jsonl` to disk |

Renaming the key would have broken the attestation route silently — nothing links the writer to the reader.

`vta_tee::did_autogen` now exports `DID_LOG_STORE_KEY` and `VTA_DID_STORE_KEY`, and every in-workspace reader takes the constant. `enclave-proxy` deliberately **cannot**: it is a separate cargo project running on the *parent* and does not link enclave code. It keeps the literal, now with a comment naming the canonical definition — an honest cross-reference rather than a fake abstraction.

Note for #827: `vta-service/src/tee_webvh.rs` introduces a fifth copy, with a doc comment justifying it as "so this bridge doesn't pull `vta-tee` into `vta-service`'s dependency graph". That rationale doesn't hold — the module is `#[cfg(feature = "tee")]` and `lib.rs` already does `pub use vta_tee as tee;` under the same feature. Whichever of these lands second should use the constant.

## 2. `parent-proxy.sh` bound the DID resolver to the IMDS port

It defaulted `VSOCK_RESOLVER_PORT` to **5400**. On the enclave side 5400 is the IMDS credential proxy and the resolver is **5600** — see `enclave-entrypoint.sh:39-40` and `enclave-proxy/src/main.rs:54,62`. A VTA brought up with this script would have had its resolver leg wired into the credential channel.

The script is also socat-only and covers four of the seven vsock channels — no storage proxy (5500), no log forwarding (5700) — so a VTA deployed with it has no persistent store and no enclave logs on the parent. The header now says that plainly and points at the Rust `enclave-proxy` as the canonical parent implementation, so nobody reaches for the socat path for a real deployment.

Surfaced by #832, which documents all seven channels correctly.

## 3. `check-changelogs.sh` could not fail the case it was written for

The guard matched the version **string anywhere in the file**, not a `<crate> <version>` entry. With a dozen subsystem crates all sitting in the 0.1.x range, patch numbers collide constantly — so `vta-tee` 0.1.0 → 0.1.1 (#819) **passed with no `vta-tee` entry at all**, because `0.1.1` already appeared for `vta-audit`, `vta-backup`, `vta-vault` and `vta-webvh`. It is now on `main` as an undocumented published version; this PR backfills the entry.

A release guard that green-lights an undocumented release is worse than no guard, because it is trusted.

The match now requires the crate name immediately before the version, accepting both heading shapes actually in use:

```
### vta-service 0.12.43 — summary
### vti-secrets 0.1.7 / vta-config 0.1.1 — summary
- `vta-audit` 0.1.1
```

The right-hand token boundary is unchanged, so a `0.1.30` entry still cannot satisfy a bump to `0.1.3`.

**Validation** — replayed the tightened guard over the last 25 commits of `main`, running it at each commit with `BASE=<commit>^`:

- **16** commits carrying version bumps still pass — no false positives.
- **1** new catch: `63539989` (#819), `MISSING vta-tee: 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1`. That is the bug, not a regression.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p vta-service --no-default-features --features tee,rest,didcomm` — clean
- `cargo check` in `deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- both release guards pass against `origin/main`

## Versions

`vta-tee` 0.1.1 → **0.1.2**, `vta-service` 0.12.42 → **0.12.45**. The gap is deliberate: #824 claims 0.12.43 and #827 claims 0.12.44, so this stays out of their way regardless of merge order.

title: docs(changelog): say which transports reach the member document form
body:
## What

Corrects one claim in the `vtc-service 0.11.37` entry from #838.

It said *"a client migrating to the document form sees no behaviour change."* That holds over **TSP and REST** and is **false over DIDComm** — which is the reading most likely to be acted on, since DIDComm is what OpenVTC sends these two verbs over today.

## Why it's wrong

`route()` matches on `msg.typ`, so `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` still reach `member_self_remove_handler` / `member_vmc_handler`, which parse a **bare body**. #838 added the document handlers to `dispatch_trust_task_core`, which DIDComm does not consult for these two types. A sender that switched to the document form without also switching transport would have its document rejected as a malformed bare body.

`join-requests/*` does not have this property — its DIDComm handlers forward to the dispatcher via `inbound_doc_bytes`, so they accept the document on every transport. That asymmetry is exactly what makes the original wording easy to misread.

## The change

- States the reachable transports outright, and names the contrast with `join-requests/*` so the asymmetry is visible.
- Splits the receipt-payload claim — which *does* hold on every transport — into its own bullet, so the two are not read as a single guarantee.

Changelog text only: no code, no version bump. `check-version-bumps.sh` excludes `CHANGELOG*` from the bump requirement; both guards re-run clean.

Refs #838, OpenVTC/openvtc#185

title: feat(vtc): dispatch self-remove and member-VMC as Trust Tasks
body:
## What

#833 gave the VTC a TSP inbound path, but that path reaches a verb **only** through `dispatch_trust_task_core`, whose table was the four `join-requests/*` URIs. The two member-initiated verbs — `members/self-remove` and `members/vmc` — existed only as DIDComm protocol-message handlers taking a bare body.

The practical effect: **a member could join a community over TSP and then not leave over it.** The frame came back `UnsupportedType`.

Both URIs were already canonical Trust Task types under `https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/members/`, so this is a routing gap rather than a spec change — the documents were always well-formed, nothing routed them.

## How

- `handle_self_remove` and `handle_member_vmc` run the document form on the **shared spine** — `remove_inner` and `receive_member_vmc_inner`, the same functions the DIDComm handlers call. The two forms therefore cannot drift on policy: the no-last-admin invariant and the VMC issuer/subject + DI-proof checks are enforced where they always were, in the effect stage.
- The proven member comes from `resolve_holder`, so the authenticated identity is the transport's (DIDComm authcrypt sender / TSP sender VID) or the document proof signer — never a self-asserted `issuer`.
- **The bare-body DIDComm handlers stay.** Existing senders keep working, and both forms return the same receipt payload, so a client migrating to the document form sees no behaviour change. Accept before send: the member-side change can only follow this, never precede it.
- `DISPATCHED_URIS` now documents what it had quietly become — the set reachable over TSP, since the TSP path has no protocol-message surface behind it — and its coverage test extends to the member verbs. The module doc no longer claims the dispatcher is join-request-only.
- `parse_disposition` moves from private to `pub(crate)` so both forms reject a bad disposition identically rather than one of them defaulting.

## Why now

Scoping OpenVTC/openvtc#185 (member-side TSP) turned up that only **one** of OpenVTC's four VTC-bound sends could ride TSP today — join submit, which already builds a Trust Task document. Self-remove and member-VMC sent bare bodies with no handler behind them on the Trust Task surface. This is the upstream half; the OpenVTC change follows it.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — 693 unit tests + every integration binary, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets`, `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `cargo check -p vtc-service --locked` — clean (lockfile committed with the bump)
- `scripts/check-version-bumps.sh`, `scripts/check-changelogs.sh` — both pass

Refs OpenVTC/openvtc#185

title: fix(vta-service): resolve self-DID via network-mode resolver in first-enable handshake
body:
## Summary

The transient "first-enable" handshake that trust-pings a newly configured mediator built a **default** TDK config, which resolves DIDs **locally**. In a serverless / network-isolated deployment the agent has no direct network egress, so resolving the mediator DID — and the VTA's own serverless `did:webvh` during mediator authentication — failed with a network error.

## Fix

- Route the first-enable handshake through the VTA's shared **network-mode** resolver (bridged to the parent-side resolver sidecar in an isolated deployment), mirroring the resolver wiring already used by the messaging service and the auth ATM.
- Re-seed the self-DID into the resolver cache immediately before the handshake: webvh cache entries expire after the cache TTL, and a serverless `did:webvh` can only be resolved from cache.

## Changes

- `vta-service/src/routes/protocol.rs` — build the handshake TDK config with the network-mode resolver + re-seed self-DID cache entry (feature-gated on `webvh`).
- `vta-service/src/server.rs` — make `preload_self_did_document` `pub(crate)` so the handshake path can reuse it.

## Testing

`cargo check -p vta-service` (default features: `setup`/`webvh` + `didcomm`) passes.

title: fix: read a join verdict at the nesting the VTC actually sends
body:
## What

A VTC's join verdict never took effect. `handle_join_verdict` deserialized the DIDComm body straight into a `VerdictResponse`, but that is not what arrives — `vtc-service`'s `tt_didcomm_reply` sets the body to the whole `#response` Trust Task **document**, with the task-specific members nested under `payload`:

```json
{ "id": "urn:uuid:…", "threadId": "…", "type": "…#response",
  "payload": { "requestId": "…", "verdict": { "effect": "allow", … } } }
```

`VerdictResponse { request_id, verdict }` has no `payload` member and both fields are required, so the parse failed, the handler logged `malformed join verdict body — ignoring`, and the membership stayed **Pending** — through an `allow` exactly as through a `deny`.

`handle_join_status_response` had the identical defect. Its handler is reached through `dispatch_trust_task_core` + `tt_didcomm_reply` too, so an `approved` status response was dropped the same way.

## Why the tests didn't catch it

They built the **bare payload** as the message body rather than the document the VTC sends — the shape the code expected, not the shape on the wire. Both handlers now have a test that constructs the real `#response` document; each fails without the fix:

```
test verdict_allow_activates ... ok                             ← bare payload (the old fiction)
test verdict_allow_activates_from_response_document ... FAILED  ← the actual wire form
```

## The fix

`trust_task_reply_payload` prefers `payload` when present and takes the body whole otherwise, so both reply shapes reach the same parse.

The two shapes are **not** distinguishable by message type — they are distinguishable by how the VTC built the reply. Anything routed through `dispatch_trust_task_core` comes back as a document; a hand-built `Reply` comes back bare. That is why `join-requests/submit-receipt` is correct as it stands (it is hand-built by `credential_present_handler`) and is deliberately left alone rather than made tolerant for symmetry's sake.

`handle_join_trust_task_error` already read `/payload/code` — it was written against the document form. Two handlers disagreeing about the same wire is what surfaced this.

## Context

Found while scoping #185. TSP delivers that same response document with **no DIDComm envelope around it**, so the handlers had to agree on the document shape before the transport could change under them — the tolerant form is what lets a TSP frame normalise into the existing dispatch unchanged. Fixing it separately because it is a live join-ceremony defect on the DIDComm path today, independent of any TSP work.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace` — all binaries green, 0 failed
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`, `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc` — clean
- `cargo check --workspace --locked` — clean

Refs #185

title: fix(vta-service): persist auto-generated serverless did:webvh record + log
body:
## Summary

In TEE mode the VTA mints its own `did:webvh` on first boot from the KMS-bootstrapped seed (`tee::did_autogen::maybe_generate_vta_did`) and stores the DID + `did.jsonl` log **only** under the `KEYS`/`BOOTSTRAP` keyspaces. That path never goes through the `create_did_webvh` flow, so the `webvh` keyspace is left empty.

But three read paths resolve the VTA's own DID from the `webvh` keyspace via `webvh_store`:
- `list_services` — reads the record (`did:{did}`) **and** log (`log:{did}`);
- `server::preload_self_did_document` — reads the log to seed the resolver cache;
- `/.well-known/did.jsonl` — reads the log.

So on a serverless TEE VTA, `GET /services` 500s with `VtaDidRecordMissing` and the VTA's own DID is unresolvable from cache — no client can authcrypt to it.

## Fix

Add a small `tee_webvh` bridge in `vta-service` that idempotently backfills the `webvh` keyspace with the record + log after auto-generation, and call it from the enclave startup right after `maybe_generate_vta_did`.

- **Idempotent**: no-op for non-`did:webvh` identities and once the entries exist, so it also repairs an already-generated DID on a rebuild + restore — without wiping state (which would rotate the DID).
- **Record fields** mirror the production serverless builder in `operations::did_webvh::create_did_webvh` (`server_id = "serverless"`, next `#key-{n}` fragment `2`, one pre-rotation key). Any drift self-heals on the next did update/rotate, which re-scans the log and persists corrected counts.
- **Log** is copied from the `KEYS`-keyspace `did.jsonl` the auto-gen already wrote.

Kept in `vta-service` (which owns `webvh_store`) rather than the low-level TEE crate, so that crate doesn't take on a `vta-webvh` dependency.

## Testing

- `cargo check -p vta-service --features tee` passes (compiles the new `#[cfg(feature = "tee")]` module + the enclave feature graph).
- `cargo test -p vta-service --features tee tee_webvh::` — new unit test for the record builder (SCID = 3rd colon-segment, fragment/pre-rotation/log counts) passes.

title: docs(security-model): re-ground the TEE security model against current code
body:
## Summary

Re-grounds `docs/01-concepts/security-model.md` against the current TEE
implementation. The document had drifted from the code in several places; this
corrects the inaccurate/stale claims and fills gaps, verified against the
implementation.

## Corrections

**Pass 1 — stale/incomplete claims:**
- **KMS attestation (Recipient):** `GenerateDataKey`/`Decrypt` now pass an
  NSM-attested `Recipient`; KMS returns `CiphertextForRecipient` wrapped
  (RSAES-OAEP-SHA256) to an ephemeral in-enclave RSA-2048 key. Updated the
  residual-risk row (was "TODO/not implemented"), the AT1 tree, added a Layer 2
  bullet + A2 mitigation and a crypto-inventory row.
- **vsock channels:** Layer 7 said "three"; the proxy actually brokers seven
  (REST, mediator, HTTPS, IMDS, storage, resolver, logs). Enumerated all and added
  the log channel to the enclave↔proxy diagram.
- **Fail-closed boot:** documented that a KMS decrypt failure only re-mints
  identity on `AccessDenied` (post-rebuild PCR0 change) or explicit
  `allow_kms_reinit`; all other error classes refuse to start.
- **Anti-rollback anchor:** added the EBS rollback / state-replay threat and its
  mitigation (external monotonic counter, config-gated) to the A2 adversary, AT3
  tree, and residual-risk table.
- **Deployment checklist:** enclave-eligible instance floor + optional
  anti-rollback anchor configuration.

**Pass 2 — six code-grounding fixes:**
- Overview: non-TEE deployments use layers 5, 6, 8 (not "4–8") — Layer 4 (config
  locking) is KMS-gated and Layer 7 (vsock) is TEE-only.
- Layer 3: storage value format is `[4-byte magic "VAE1"][12-byte nonce][ciphertext
  + 16-byte GCM tag]`, AAD-bound to its `(keyspace, key)` location.
- Layer 5 / A2: the DID-method restriction is an optional allowlist (TEE-only, off
  by default) enforced at auth time — it does not unconditionally block `did:web`.
- Trust Boundaries: fjall storage physically lives on the parent EBS (semi-trusted);
  the enclave holds only the storage-encryption key in memory.
- Attack tree: KMS `Decrypt` uses end-to-end TLS enclave↔KMS over a CONNECT tunnel
  not terminated by the parent; `webpki-roots` is the proxy's mediator/resolver
  trust store, not the KMS path.
- Crypto inventory: add AES-256-CBC (KMS `CiphertextForRecipient` CMS content
  encryption).

Docs-only; no crate sources or versions touched.

title: perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list (#826)
body:
perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list (#826)

The Nitro builder stage's dependency-cache warm-up only listed 9 of the
workspace's 26 members, so the manifest-first `cargo build` under-populated
the cache and dependencies were rebuilt from scratch on every image build.
It also copied only a subset of crates for the real build.

Restore selective per-crate manifest + dummy-source + real-source COPYs for
ALL workspace members (kind matched to each manifest: bin/lib/both, plus
vta-mobile-core's uniffi-bindgen bin), and keep deploy/nitro/config.toml baked
only in Stage 2. Editing config now re-layers just the tiny Alpine runtime
stage instead of invalidating the entire Rust dependency cache. Portable — no
BuildKit or cache mounts required.

Notably, the tests-only `tests/e2e` member (`autobins = false`, integration
tests only) has no compile target until its real sources are copied, so it
gets a stub `src/lib.rs` in the warm-up phase purely to satisfy workspace
resolution — without it, `cargo build` fails resolution and the `|| true`
silently swallows the error, giving a full-from-scratch dependency rebuild
every time.

Also exclude enclave signing keys and Nitro runtime state from the build
context (.dockerignore): the build uses selective per-crate COPYs, but adding
`signing/`, `.deploy-nitro/`, and stray `*.txt` avoids shipping private keys
and large EIF artifacts to the Docker daemon.

title: perf(deploy/nitro): per-crate COPY layering + full workspace manifest list
body:
## Summary

The Nitro enclave image (`Dockerfile.nitro`) uses a manifest-first dependency-cache warm-up: copy every crate's `Cargo.toml` + a stub source, run a dummy `cargo build` to compile & cache all external dependencies, then copy the real sources. This only works if the stub phase lists **every** workspace member — otherwise `cargo build` fails workspace resolution, the `|| true` swallows the error, and dependencies are rebuilt from scratch on every image build.

The stub list had drifted to only **9 of the 26** workspace members, and the real-source copy covered the same subset.

## Fix

- List **all** workspace members for both the manifest/stub phase and the real-source copy, with the stub target kind matched to each crate's manifest (bin / lib / both; plus `vta-mobile-core`'s `uniffi-bindgen` bin).
- Keep `deploy/nitro/config.toml` baked only in Stage 2 (runtime). Never `COPY . .` in Stage 1, so editing config re-layers just the tiny Alpine stage instead of invalidating the Rust dependency cache.
- `tests/e2e` (`autobins = false`, integration tests only) has no compile target until its real sources are copied, so it gets a stub `src/lib.rs` in the warm-up phase purely to satisfy workspace resolution. **This was the actual bug** — without a target, `cargo metadata`/`cargo build` fails with `no targets specified in the manifest`.

## `.dockerignore`

Exclude `signing/` (enclave signing cert + private key), `.deploy-nitro/` (EIF artifacts, logs, pidfiles), and stray `*.txt` from the build context — avoids shipping private keys and large EIF artifacts to the Docker daemon.

## Testing

Reconstructed the Stage-1 stub layout (root manifest + `Cargo.lock` + all 26 member manifests + stub sources) in a scratch dir and confirmed `cargo metadata` (full dependency resolution) exits 0 — i.e. the warm-up `cargo build` resolves the workspace instead of silently failing. Verified the member list is an exact 1:1 match with `[workspace].members`.

title: fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32 (#819)
body:
fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32 (#819)

The Nitro Security Module ioctl expects `struct nsm_iovec { __u64 addr;
__u64 len; }`. Declaring `len` as u32 under #[repr(C)] leaves 4 bytes of
uninitialized padding that the kernel reads as the high bits of the
64-bit length, inflating it to a garbage value and failing the ioctl
with EMSGSIZE (os error 90). Use u64 for both the request and response
buffer lengths.

title: fix(vta-tee): NSM ioctl len field must be u64, not u32
body:
## Summary

Fixes the AWS Nitro Security Module (NSM) ioctl request encoding used by the
enclave attestation path.

## The bug

The NSM ioctl takes `struct nsm_iovec { __u64 addr; __u64 len; }`. The Rust
binding declared `len` as `u32`:

```rust
#[repr(C)]
struct NsmIoBuffer {
    addr: u64,
    len: u32,   // 4 bytes of trailing padding under #[repr(C)]
}
```

Under `#[repr(C)]` the `u32` is followed by 4 bytes of **uninitialized**
padding to satisfy 8-byte alignment. The kernel reads the full 8 bytes as the
`__u64` length, so the padding becomes the high bits — inflating the length to
a garbage value and failing the ioctl with `EMSGSIZE` (os error 90).

## The fix

Declare `len` as `u64` (matching the kernel struct) and widen the two length
assignments accordingly. The struct size is unchanged (`0x20`), so the
`NSM_IOCTL_REQUEST` request code is unaffected.

## Testing

- `cargo check -p vta-tee` passes.
- Verified live on an AWS Nitro Enclave: attestation succeeds and
  `/attestation/status` reports `tee_type: nitro, detected: true`.

title: feat(vtc): accept Trust Tasks over TSP
body:
§6.1/§6.2 of `docs/05-design-notes/tsp-enablement.md` for the VTC — PR 6 of the §13 breakdown. Behind the `tsp` feature, off by default.

## The bug this fixes is a silent drop

TSP frames **already reach the VTC**. The delivery-layer `DidCommTransport` owns the one mediator websocket and surfaces both protocols off it, tagging each `Inbound.message.protocol`. The dispatcher then discarded every TSP frame at its first line:

```rust
let msg: Message = serde_json::from_slice(&inbound.message.payload).ok()?;
```

A TSP payload is Trust-Task bytes, not a DIDComm plaintext — so this returned `None` and the frame vanished **with no log line**.

## What it does

Mirrors `vta-service`'s `messaging::tsp_inbound` + `service::handle_tsp` deliberately rather than inventing a shape: TSP, DIDComm and REST all feed `dispatch_trust_task_core`, so a caller gets identical round-trip semantics whichever transport it arrived on.

- **`Protocol::TSP` → `handle_tsp`**, which dispatches on the shared spine and seals the response back to the proven sender over the same socket (`atm.tsp().send_routed([mediator_did, sender_vid])`). **No second websocket** — the mediator permits one per DID and evicts a second as `duplicate-channel`, which is what flapped the VTA before its standalone loop was removed.
- **Authorization**: the caller is the VID TSP's `unpack` authenticated, and **only** when `verified` is set.
- **Unauthorised → error envelope, not silence.** The VID is cryptographically proven so there's no enumeration exposure, and a conformant client only understands envelopes.
- `JoinTransport::Tsp` records the arrival transport.

## Two decisions worth review

**No plaintext-`from` fallback.** The DIDComm path has one, for two public-read handlers that never authorize on it. TSP has no such reader, so accepting an unproven identity here would only create a way in.

**`tsp_sender` is factored out** so the authorization decision is unit-testable without a mediator socket — the same reason `vta-service` factors out `inbound_gate`. `dispatch_trust_task_core` authorises on its return value, so a wrong answer there is an authorization bug, not a logging one. Three tests pin it: verified sender accepted, unverified refused, anonymous refused.

## Scope: receive-side only

Per §14 Q4 — answering over TSP is required (the caller waits on the TSP correlation), but VTC-**initiated** sends to members stay DIDComm until the Phase B flip (§12).

## Deliberately NOT advertised

The VTC's DID document still carries no `#tsp` service, and must not until this ships. TSP is the **highest-preference** transport, so a VTC advertising it before it could answer would have clients select TSP and get silence — strictly worse than today, and the same false-capability problem the OpenVTC panel work fixed.

Advertising then needs **no code**: it's an `update_did_webvh` service patch on the VTA-managed VTC DID (`operations/did_webvh/update/` already patches arbitrary `/service` blocks). That's the follow-up, and it unblocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2f.

## Verification

- **Both feature configurations build**: default and `--features tsp`
- **695 lib tests pass in each** (3 new on the authorization gate)

title: feat(vtc): accept Trust Tasks over TSP (#833)
body:
feat(vtc): accept Trust Tasks over TSP (#833)

* feat(vtc): accept Trust Tasks over TSP

TSP frames already reached the VTC. The delivery-layer DidCommTransport owns
the one mediator websocket and surfaces both protocols off it, tagging each
Inbound.message.protocol. The dispatcher then dropped every TSP frame
SILENTLY at its first line: a TSP payload is Trust-Task bytes, not a DIDComm
plaintext, so serde_json::from_slice::<Message>(..).ok()? returned None and
the frame vanished with no log.

This is §6.1/§6.2 of docs/05-design-notes/tsp-enablement.md for the VTC. It
mirrors vta-service's messaging::tsp_inbound + service::handle_tsp
deliberately rather than inventing a shape: TSP, DIDComm and REST all feed
dispatch_trust_task_core, so a caller gets identical round-trip semantics
whichever transport it arrived on.

  * Protocol::TSP routes to handle_tsp, which dispatches on the shared spine
    and seals the response back to the proven sender over the same socket
    (atm.tsp().send_routed([mediator_did, sender_vid])). No second
    websocket -- the mediator permits one per DID and evicts a second as
    duplicate-channel, which is what flapped the VTA before its standalone
    loop was removed.

  * The caller identity is the VID TSP's unpack authenticated, and only when
    `verified` is set. tsp_sender is factored out so that decision is
    unit-testable without a mediator socket -- the same reason vta-service
    factors out inbound_gate. There is deliberately NO plaintext-`from`
    fallback: the DIDComm path has one for two public-read handlers that
    never authorize on it, and TSP has no such reader, so accepting an
    unproven identity would only create a way in.

  * An unauthorised caller gets a Trust-Task error envelope, not silence.
    The VID is cryptographically proven so there is no enumeration exposure,
    and a conformant client only understands envelopes.

  * JoinTransport::Tsp records the arrival transport.

Receive-side only, per §14 Q4: answering over TSP is required (the caller is
waiting on the TSP correlation), but VTC-initiated sends to members stay
DIDComm until the Phase B flip.

Behind the `tsp` feature, still off by default; the feature now also enables
affinidi-tdk/tsp for atm.tsp(), routed through a dependency vtc-service
already has rather than adding affinidi-messaging-sdk directly.

NOT advertised yet, and must not be until this ships: TSP is the
highest-preference transport, so a VTC advertising #tsp before it could
answer would have clients select it and get silence -- strictly worse than
today. Advertising needs no code; it is an update_did_webvh service patch on
the VTA-managed VTC DID.

Verified: both feature configurations build and pass 695 lib tests (3 new on
the authorization gate); clippy -D warnings clean in both; fmt clean.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(vtc): give the admission-credential wait a CI-sized bound

`didcomm_join_round_trips_submit_manifest_status_approve_and_vmc_delivery`
awaits two independently-pushed credentials (the VMC and the role VEC) with
a 20s bound each. That is comfortable locally -- the whole test runs in ~6s
-- and marginal on a runner, where it takes ~23s.

The marginality is not hypothetical. The same assertion at the same line has
failed CI on unrelated PRs, including #825 whose entire diff was a `pub use`
re-export line: nothing in it could reach a DIDComm join. Both times the test
passed locally 3/3. So the bound was what broke, not the code, and
re-running until it lands is not a fix.

Raised to 60s behind a named constant, with the reasoning at both the
constant and the assertion. Still bounded -- a genuine hang still fails
rather than hanging the job -- just past where runner slowness lives. The
assertion already carried a comment about an earlier CI flake here (arrival
order), so this is the second time this test has needed hardening against
the same environment.

Separate commit from the TSP work in this PR deliberately: it is a test-only
change that happens to unblock it.

0.11.36 (#834 had taken 0.11.35), and Cargo.lock needs to move with it or
CI's --locked jobs refuse. Verified with --locked this time rather than
relying on checks that let cargo rewrite the lock silently.

title: feat(credential-exchange): the issuance and presentation family, 0.1
body:
Adds `credential-exchange/{offer,request,issue,query,present}/0.1` and `credential-exchange/pending/{list,approve,deny}/0.1`, plus the shared `credential-exchange/_shared/0.1/deferred-presentation`.

## Why now

These eight URIs are bound and dispatched today by `vta-sdk` / `vta-service` / `vtc-service`, but they resolve to nothing. The five exchange specs exist only as files in the OpenVTC repo while claiming a `trusttasks.org` ID; the three `pending-*` have no spec anywhere. See OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#821 — it is the same published-authority-claim problem that #710 just finished fixing for `spec/vtc/*`, one family later.

## Shape

**The Trust Task is the transport, authentication, threading and relayer envelope; the body is OID4VCI (issuance) or OID4VP + DCQL (presentation).** Those foreign objects are carried verbatim and deliberately **not** re-specified here — re-stating another specification's shape inside this one creates a second source of truth that drifts the moment it revises. `snake_case` members in the schemas (`credential_offer`, `dcql_query`, `vp_token`) are those specifications' own names, not casing drift.

The five exchange tasks are **one-way messages on a thread**, so they declare no `Response` — following `chat/message` and `sync/event`. The `pending/*` trio are request/response and declare one.

## The pending/* trio

When a verifier the holder has not pre-trusted sends a query, the holder neither answers nor refuses — it **defers**, persists the request, and tells the verifier `consentRequired`. These three are how the decision then gets made out of band: list what is waiting, then approve or deny.

They are nested under `pending/` rather than published as flat `pending-list` / `pending-approve` / `pending-deny` siblings of the protocol tasks. The family then reads as what it is: a party-to-party wire protocol, plus an operator surface over the consent backlog it generates.

## Three properties worth reviewing

Each is a rule a plausible implementation gets wrong by default, so each is stated normatively rather than left to inference:

- **`purpose` on a query is REQUIRED and non-empty.** The holder's decision is a consent decision, and consent to an unstated use is not consent. Making it optional would render the well-behaved verifier's query indistinguishable from the one that declines to say — exactly when the difference matters.
- **No wallet enumeration.** Candidates are gathered *only* through the type index named by the query's `meta` discriminator. The consequence is spelled out because it inverts the intuitive reading: a query carrying **no** discriminator contributes **no** candidates. It does not mean "everything". Relatedly, `noMatch` and "held but not consented" must be indistinguishable to the verifier, or refusal itself becomes an enumeration primitive.
- **A denial carries no reason field**, and rejects unknown members. "I don't hold that" and "I hold it and won't show you" have to stay indistinguishable, and a free-text reason is where that leaks.

## pending/approve is `destructive`

Not for what it deletes, but because the disclosure it causes cannot be walked back — there is no revoking a presentation once the verifier holds it.

It mints against the **original** query and nonce. The payload is an `id` and nothing else, so approval is a yes-or-no on a request already made rather than an opportunity to renegotiate it; otherwise the thing approved and the thing presented could differ, which makes the consent record worthless as evidence. An expired deferral MUST be refused rather than re-nonced — silently substituting a fresh nonce presents against a request the verifier has forgotten making, on an authority nobody re-confirmed.

`present/0.1` also states an asymmetry it would be easy to gloss over: plain `eddsa-jcs-2022` has no claim-level selective disclosure, so a holder MUST refuse that path unless the credential's claims are a subset of what was consented to. Over-disclosure there is silent unless explicitly checked for.

## Renumbering and nesting

The five exchange tasks move `1.0` → `0.1`, and `pending-list` → `pending/list`. Both match how the rest of the registry versions and groups its slugs. The consuming repo renames its constants in a follow-up; there are no external consumers, so the wire change is free.

## Also in this PR

Nothing beyond the specs and the regenerated bindings.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 256 specs (248 before), 46 shared schemas
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen` + `cargo fmt --all` — no drift
- `npm run build-ts-bindings` — 302 TS modules
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate` — clean (this is where invalid-example conformance runs; every invalid example is genuinely rejected by its schema)
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs` — clean
- `tsc --noEmit` — clean

Versions bumped in step: `trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.41, `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.2.41.

title: feat(vtc)!: repoint config export/import, retiring the last openvtc/vtc bindings (#710)
body:
Closes #710.

`admin/config/{export,import}` move to the canonical `spec/vtc/config/{export,import}/0.1` authored upstream in [trust-tasks-tf#147](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/147) (`trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.40, pinned here).

They were the last two bindings on `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/`. **That authority is now unbound across the whole workspace** — router, `vta-sdk` constants, admin SPA and `cnm-cli` alike:

```
$ grep -rhoE '"https://trusttasks\.org/openvtc/vtc/[^"]+"' \
    vtc-service/src vta-sdk/src cnm-cli/src vtc-service/admin-ui/src | wc -l
0
```

All 66 entries in `trust-tasks/index.json` are `retired` with a `supersededBy`, which turns that file from a manifest into a redirect table for anyone still holding an old URI. Both census tables in `vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs` — `AWAITING_CANONICAL_FOLD` and `UNBOUND_OK` — are now empty, and `no_new_bindings_on_the_retired_authority` is what stops it regressing one literal at a time.

## Why these two took the longest

They were the only entries in the whole migration whose recorded blocker was **real**: no canonical counterpart existed. `specs/config/` published `show`, `patch`, `reload`, `restart` and nothing to migrate to.

But the fix that blocker proposed — push `communityProfile` into `ext` and promote these into the generic `config/*` family — was still wrong. `communityProfile` and its diff are roughly half the import's payload, so the "generic" task would have been a hollow shell in its only real use. They are `vtc/`-slugged instead, on the `vtc/backup/{export,import}` precedent.

That is the pattern across #710 as a whole, and it is recorded in the design note and the now-empty fold table so it isn't relearned: of the ten dispositions on file, most of the blockers did not survive contact. Three assumed a `confirm/1.0` gate that could not apply (it is asynchronous; those flows verify in-band via WebAuthn), one named a target task that would have reintroduced a policy bypass, one assumed an endpoint had to survive when nothing called it, and one cited a duplicate relationship that did not exist. **Verify a blocker before planning work on it.**

## Breaking wire changes

The repoint is not a rename:

- **`confirm` moves from the query string into the payload.** A Trust Task is one interface over REST, DIDComm and TSP, and only REST has a query string to carry a flag in. A stale client still sending `?confirm=true` now **previews** instead of applying — the recoverable direction. Pinned by `import_ignores_the_pre_migration_confirm_query_param`.
- **Export wraps its result**: `{ "document": { … } }` rather than the bare document. The registry response convention needs `additionalProperties: false` plus an `ext` extension point, and neither attaches to a bare `$ref`.
- **Import returns one shape with a discriminant.** `confirmed: bool` → `status: "preview" | "imported"`; `communityProfileDiff` → `profileChanges`; `configOverridesDiff` → `overrideChanges`. The `communityProfileApplied` / `configOverridesApplied` lists are **gone** — on `imported` the change arrays carry what was actually written, so a key that failed to persist lands in `rejected` rather than being reported as applied.
- **`pendingRestart` is new, and is reported on the preview too** — an operator learns that confirming implies downtime while they are still deciding whether to confirm. Pinned by `import_preview_reports_pending_restart_before_confirming`.
- **Absent-vs-null is preserved on the wire.** `oldValue` / `newValue` are omitted when unset rather than emitted as `null`, so "leave this field alone" stays distinguishable from an explicit "clear it". Conflating those turns every partial document into a destructive one.

No SPA or CLI consumer existed for either endpoint, so the blast radius is external callers only.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace` clean (as CI runs it)
- Full `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vti-common`: 52 test binaries, exit 0, zero failures (built with the admin UI, not `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD`)
- `every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry` resolves both new URIs against the published `trust_tasks_rs` 0.2.40 rather than a hand-maintained list, so a typo or an unauthored slug would fail here rather than at runtime

`vtc-service` 0.11.35.

title: VTC Trust Task URIs conform to neither the public nor the private Type URI form (SPEC 6.1 / 6.5)
body:
Found while reconciling `trust-tasks/index.json` against the router (#537 follow-up). Not fixed there — every VTC task URI is a wire type, so changing the shape is a breaking change for every client and needs a decision before any code moves.

## The two conformant forms

Per the published framework (`dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`, SPEC 6.1 / 6.5):

- **Public registry:** `https://trusttasks.org/spec/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>`. The `/spec/` segment is structural, not decorative — 6.1 defines slug resolution as "the segments between `/spec/` and the version".
- **Private/internal:** the *same URI shape* under **a different authority**. 6.5 rule 1 is explicit that a private spec's Type URI **MUST NOT** be served from, or claim to identify a resource at, the `https://trusttasks.org/` domain — that domain is reserved for specs published through the public registry process.

## What VTC emits

Two shapes, neither conformant, both under `trusttasks.org`:

**1. Flat form — 66 of 71 manifest entries.** e.g. `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/members/list/1.0`. No `/spec/` segment, so a consumer following 6.1 cannot parse the slug at all. This is already known to break the framework parser: `vta-sdk/src/protocols/join_requests.rs:17-21` records that the flat form "deserialised as a `&str` but failed `serde_json::from_slice::<TrustTask<Value>>`" — which is why the join-request family was migrated.

**2. Migrated form — the 5 join-request tasks.** e.g. `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/spec/join-requests/submit/1.0`. Parses as a `TypeUri`, so it fixed the deserialization defect. But the authority is still `trusttasks.org` with `openvtc/vtc` as extra path segments — that is not the public-registry form (which has no org segments) and not the private form (which requires a different authority). The doc comment there cites "6.5 private registry" as justification; 6.5 is the section that forbids using this domain for private specs.

So the migration fixed parsing without resolving the authority question, and 66 entries never got even that.

## The decision

Two coherent end states, and the choice is governance, not engineering:

- **Public:** submit the VTC slugs through the public registry process (6.5 item 5) and re-publish as `https://trusttasks.org/spec/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>`, dropping `openvtc/vtc` from the path. Slug collision across orgs becomes a real constraint.
- **Private:** move to an authority OpenVTC controls — e.g. `https://openvtc.org/trust-tasks/<slug>/<MAJOR.MINOR>` — keeping the shape and dropping the claim on `trusttasks.org`.

Worth noting 6.5 item 5 explicitly: the private URI and a later public URI "identify distinct specifications unless and until the registry policy explicitly aliases them". So picking private now is not a free migration to public later.

## Scope once decided

Breaking for every client. `type` values on the wire, the `Trust-Task` header, 71 manifest ids + on-disk dirs, `vta-sdk` constants (published crate), and any external consumer. Needs the versioning-and-migration dance in SPEC 5.4 (publish new, dual-accept, retire old with `supersededBy`) rather than a rename.

Blocks #709 — publishing 20 more tasks in a shape that is about to change means doing that work twice.

title: feat(vtc): config export/import 0.1 — portable community configuration
body:
Adds `vtc/config/export/0.1` and `vtc/config/import/0.1`, plus the shared `vtc/_shared/0.1/config-portability` they both use.

These are the last two Trust Tasks `vtc-service` still binds on the retired `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` authority (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#710). Everything else on that authority has migrated; `admin/config/{export,import}` could not, because `specs/config/` publishes `show`, `patch`, `reload` and `restart` and no export/import counterpart existed to migrate *to*. This authors it.

## What the tasks do

**`vtc/config/export`** returns a community's portable configuration — its profile and its stored configuration overrides — as one self-describing document.

It takes no parameters. `config/show` has a `keys` selector because an operator inspecting a running maintainer often wants one key; an export does not, because a document carrying an arbitrary subset is not portable. Importing one would silently leave the unselected keys at whatever the target already had, which is the failure the task exists to avoid.

**`vtc/config/import`** applies that document, or previews what applying it would change. `confirm` defaults to `false`, so the outcome of a forgotten member is a preview rather than an overwritten community. `rejected` is populated on the preview too — a rejection discovered *after* writing the accepted half leaves a community matching neither the old configuration nor the imported one.

## Why VTC-slugged rather than generic `config/*`

The prior plan was to promote these into the generic `config/*` family with the community profile pushed into `ext`. That is dropped: `communityProfile` and its `profileChanges` diff are roughly half the import's payload, so a generic task with them in an opaque vendor namespace would be a hollow shell in its only real use.

`vtc/backup/{export,import}/0.1` set the precedent — VTC-shaped state operations get a `vtc/` slug, carry `confirm` in the payload rather than a query string, and keep their fields first-class. These follow it.

## Two shape decisions worth review

**`CommunityProfileSnapshot` is deliberately not `vtc/_shared/0.1/community`'s `CommunityProfile`.** That one is the update-facing view and omits `communityDid` precisely so a patch cannot re-point a community's identity. The snapshot **requires** it, because the DID is what lets an import refuse a document taken from a different community. The import reads it for that comparison and never writes it — nor `createdAt`. A consumer with no profile yet accepts any DID, which is the standing-up-a-replacement case.

**`schemaVersion` inside a versioned Type URI is not redundant.** The URI versions the *envelope*. The moment an operator writes the response to a file the envelope is gone and the document is bare JSON, so `schemaVersion` is the only thing a later reader — possibly a different implementation, possibly across a version boundary — has to check it against. Same principle as `BackupEnvelope` carrying its KDF parameters in the clear.

Both specs also pin the omission rule explicitly: a field the document omits is left alone, **not** cleared. A caller clearing a nullable member sends an explicit `null`. Conflating the two turns every partial document into a destructive one.

## Tooling fix included

This change tripped over a latent bug in the TS binding generator. Shared-module aliases are derived from basename + version and do **not** distinguish families, so `config/_shared/0.1/config` and a `vtc/_shared/0.1/config` both want `ConfigShared_v0_1`. The generator emitted both, and `tsc` failed with a `TS2300` in generated code — a diagnostic pointing at the symptom that names neither colliding spec.

The generator now raises at generation time with both paths:

```
Error: duplicate TS export alias(es) — rename one of the colliding shared schemas
(the alias comes from the file's basename + version, not its family):
  ConfigShared_v0_1: ./config/_shared/0.1/config vs ./vtc/_shared/0.1/config
```

Verified by reintroducing the collision deliberately. The shared schema here is named `config-portability` rather than `config` for the same reason: a family-qualified alias scheme would rename every existing shared export (`BackupShared_v0_1` → `VtcBackupShared_v0_1`, etc.) and break TS consumers, so the collision is avoided by name instead. Worth a maintainer opinion on whether the rename-the-scheme route is preferable long-term.

## Housekeeping

`trust-tasks-ts/package-lock.json` was stale at `0.2.38` against a `0.2.39` `package.json`. Regenerating it as part of this bump brings both to `0.2.40`.

## Verification

- `npm run validate` — 248 specs, 45 shared schemas

title: feat(vtc): config export/import 0.1 — portable community configuration (#147)
body:
feat(vtc): config export/import 0.1 — portable community configuration (#147)

Adds `vtc/config/export/0.1` and `vtc/config/import/0.1`, plus the shared
`vtc/_shared/0.1/config-portability` they both use.

Export returns a community's portable configuration — its profile and its
stored configuration overrides — as one self-describing document. It takes
no parameters: `config/show` has a `keys` selector because an operator
inspecting a running maintainer often wants one key, but a document carrying
an arbitrary subset is not portable, since importing it would silently leave
the unselected keys at whatever the target already had.

Import applies that document, or previews what applying it would change.
`confirm` defaults to `false`, so the outcome of a forgotten member is a
preview rather than an overwritten community. `rejected` is populated on the
preview too — a rejection discovered after writing the accepted half leaves a
community matching neither the old configuration nor the imported one.

Two shape decisions worth stating:

`CommunityProfileSnapshot` is deliberately not `vtc/_shared/0.1/community`'s
`CommunityProfile`. That one is the update-facing view and omits
`communityDid` so a patch cannot re-point a community's identity. The
snapshot REQUIRES it, because the DID is what lets an import refuse a
document taken from a different community. The import reads it for that
comparison and never writes it — nor `createdAt`.

`schemaVersion` inside a versioned Type URI is not redundant. The URI
versions the envelope; the moment an operator writes the response to a file
the envelope is gone and the document is bare JSON, so `schemaVersion` is the
only thing a later reader has to check it against.

These supersede the non-conformant `openvtc/vtc/admin/config/{export,import}/1.0`
that `vtc-service` still binds (VTI #710) — the last two bindings on that
retired authority. They are VTC-slugged rather than folded into the generic
`config/*` family: `communityProfile` and its diff are roughly half the
import's payload, so a generic task with those pushed into `ext` would be a
hollow shell in its only real use. Same reasoning that put
`vtc/backup/{export,import}` under `vtc/`.

Also fixes the TS binding generator, which this change tripped over. Shared
module aliases are derived from basename + version and do not distinguish
families, so `config/_shared/0.1/config` and a `vtc/_shared/0.1/config` both
want `ConfigShared_v0_1`. The generator emitted both and `tsc` failed with a
TS2300 in generated code — a diagnostic that names neither colliding spec. It
now raises at generation time with both paths. The shared schema here is
named `config-portability` rather than `config` for the same reason: a
family-qualified alias scheme would rename every existing shared export and
break TS consumers, so the collision is avoided by name instead.

`trust-tasks-ts/package-lock.json` was stale at 0.2.38 against a 0.2.39
`package.json`; regenerating it as part of the bump brings both to 0.2.40.

title: docs(tee): document the serverless did:webvh identity lifecycle
body:
## Summary

Documents two load-bearing but previously-undocumented properties of a **serverless
TEE VTA** — one that sets `[tee.kms].vta_did_template` and mints its own `did:webvh`
from the enclave seed instead of publishing a `did.jsonl` to a hosting endpoint:

1. **The auto-generated DID record + log must be persisted to the `webvh`
   keyspace**, not only the key-material store, because `GET /services`, the self-DID
   resolver preload at startup, and `GET /.well-known/did.jsonl` all resolve the
   VTA's own DID from that keyspace.
2. **A serverless `did:webvh` is resolvable only from the local resolver cache** —
   there is no hosting endpoint and the enclave has no direct network egress, so all
   resolution routes through the parent-side network-mode resolver sidecar, and the
   self-DID is re-seeded into cache before the first-enable mediator handshake.

## Changes

- Add the `maybe_generate_vta_did()` → `webvh`-keyspace backfill step to the TEE
  startup sequence in `docs/02-vta/tee-architecture.md`.
- Add a new **"Self-issued did:webvh identity and resolution"** subsection.

Docs-only; no crate sources or versions touched.

title: feat(vtc)!: retire admin-login and the legacy config surface (#710)
body:
Closes two of the last four bindings on the retired
`https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` authority. Both turned out to be
**deletions**, not the folds the design note recorded — and both recorded
blockers were wrong, which is why they sat unresolved.

## `auth/admin-login` — the blocker assumed the endpoint had to survive

Recorded as "collapse into `auth/authenticate`, cookie side-effect moves to a
binding/`ext`". But `POST /v1/auth/admin-login` ran the *same*
`authenticate_and_mint` as `POST /v1/auth/` and differed only by appending
`Set-Cookie` — and that cookie half is already a canonical task:
`POST /v1/auth/admin-session` (`spec/vtc/auth/admin-session/0.1`) validates an
access token the caller holds and mints the same `vtc_admin_session` + `csrf`
pair.

So login is `spec/auth/authenticate/0.1` then `admin-session` — no binding
extension needed, and the `Trust-Task` value still distinguishes a cookie mint
from a bearer one for SIEM filtering, which was the separate ID's whole
justification. Removed rather than repointed because **nothing called it**: the
admin SPA already logs in this way (`admin-ui/src/lib/wallet.ts` →
`pages/Login.tsx`), and no test, CLI or SDK path referenced it. Passkey login
(`/v1/auth/passkey-login/finish`) mints the cookies directly and is unchanged.

## `config/legacy/manage` — the recorded reason was wrong twice over

It read "strict duplicate of `admin/config/manage`, which shipped". That task
was itself retired, and the two surfaces never shared a single field:
`/v1/config` carried community identity, `/v1/admin/config` carries
`server.host` / `server.port` / `log.level`.

The deletion rests on a field-by-field ownership audit instead:

| Legacy field | Canonical owner |
|---|---|
| `vtc_did` | `communityDid` on `spec/vtc/community/profile/show/0.1` — any authenticated session, the same reach the legacy `GET` had |
| `vtc_name`, `vtc_description` | `spec/vtc/community/profile/{show,update}/0.1`, already the sole write path the legacy `PATCH` delegated to |
| `public_url` | the `config_store` db-overlay, read by `spec/config/show/0.1` and written by `spec/config/patch/0.1` — the same overlay the legacy `PATCH` wrote |

The legacy handler's `409` on `vtc_did` / `vta_did` went away with it, so the
guarantee it enforced is now pinned on the successors — where it holds
**structurally** rather than by a runtime branch: `CommunityProfileUpdate` has
no `community_did` field, and neither identity key is in the config-store
`REGISTRY`, so a patch naming them is rejected as an unknown key. New suite
`vtc-service/tests/config_identity.rs` asserts exactly that, plus the
`public_url` overlay round-trip the retired `tests/config_legacy.rs` covered
(`admin_config.rs` exercises pending-restart with `server.port`; this does it
with the key the legacy PATCH actually wrote).

## Both census tables are empty now

`UNBOUND_OK` held seven shared-mount exceptions. Five had been retired as their
families moved to `spec/vtc/*` — and the assertion skips retired entries, so
those rows were dead weight. The remaining two were `draft` rows on the retired
authority describing routes that had **already** migrated:
`GET /v1/endorsement-types` enforces `spec/vtc/endorsement-types/register/0.1`,
`DELETE /v1/members/{did}/personhood` enforces
`spec/vtc/members/personhood/assert/0.1`. Both retired against the canonical
`list/0.1` / `revoke/0.1` the registry publishes.

Those two mounts still collapse a second verb onto a sibling's canonical task.
The fan-out is unblocked (Phase 2c established that `task_routes` layers the
method router), but it is a canonical-side split rather than an authority
migration, so it is left for its own change.

## What's left, and why it isn't backlog

`admin/config/{export,import}` are blocked on an upstream spec that does not
exist — `specs/config/` publishes `show`, `patch`, `reload`, `restart` and no
export/import counterpart.

The earlier plan to promote them as a generic `config/{export,import}` with
`communityProfile` pushed into `ext` is **dropped**: `communityProfileDiff` /
`communityProfileApplied` are roughly half the import response, so the generic
task would be a hollow shell in its only real use.
`vtc/backup/{export,import}/0.1` is the precedent for the alternative —
VTC-slugged, `confirm` carried in the payload rather than a query string,
fields first-class. Target is `spec/vtc/config/{export,import}/0.1`, to be
authored in `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf`; the repoint here follows that release.

## Also in this branch

`fix(vta-sdk)`: `DIDCommSession::receive_next`'s poll loop denied
`clippy::never_loop` whenever the `tsp` feature was off — its only `continue`
is `#[cfg(feature = "tsp")]`, so everything else returns and the loop runs
once. Annotated `#[cfg_attr(not(feature = "tsp"), allow(clippy::never_loop))]`
so the lint stays live where it can still catch a real regression. This was a
**latent CI break**: `tsp` is off by default in `vta-service`, so
`cargo clippy --workspace` builds `vta-sdk` without it too — CI has been green
only because its stable toolchain predates the lint firing here.
`cargo clippy -p vtc-service` already failed hard.

## Breaking changes

`POST /v1/auth/admin-login` and `GET, PATCH /v1/config` are removed. Use
`POST /v1/auth/` + `POST /v1/auth/admin-session`, and
`GET/PUT /v1/community/profile` + `GET/PATCH /v1/admin/config`.

## Verification

- `cargo fmt --check` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace` clean (as CI runs it), and `cargo clippy -p vtc-service -p vti-common --all-targets` clean
- Full `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vti-common`: 52 test binaries, exit 0, zero failures (built with the admin UI, not `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD`)
- `cargo test -p vta-sdk` green

Versions bumped: `vtc-service` 0.11.34, `vti-common` 0.11.27, `vta-sdk` 0.20.5.

title: chore: reach resolve_vta_with_resolver at its canonical path
body:
Cleanup that #198 flagged. **No behaviour change** — same function, same call, shorter path.

## What

#198 had to import `resolve_vta_with_resolver` through `provision_client::resolve::`, because `provision_client` re-exported `resolve_vta` but not its `_with_resolver` sibling — an asymmetry introduced upstream with the function itself (mine, in VTI #813). VTI #825 fixed the re-export and shipped in **vta-sdk 0.20.6**, so the workaround and the comment explaining it both go.

## The version floor now says why

Rather than just naming the latest release, the comment records what each step buys:

- **0.20.2** — first offered the TSP leg (earlier 0.20.x only had `connect_tsp`, which opens its own websocket and is unusable for a client already holding a DIDComm session)
- **0.20.3** — the resolver-injection seam the discovery tests need (VTI #813)
- **0.20.6** — exports it from `provision_client` rather than only its inner module (VTI #825)

So someone lowering the pin later can see which capability they'd lose.

title: VtaClient::sign() is the only signing entry point that cannot reach TSP
body:
`keys.rs` has three signing entry points. Two of them route through the Trust-Task bridge and therefore work on every transport; the primary one does not.

| Method | Routes via | Works on TSP |
|---|---|---|
| `derive_and_sign` | `rpc_tt(TASK_KEYS_DERIVE_AND_SIGN_1_0, …)` (`vta-sdk/src/client/keys.rs:149`) | yes |
| `derive_and_sign_document` | `rpc_tt(TASK_KEYS_DERIVE_AND_SIGN_DOCUMENT_1_0, …)` (`keys.rs:176`) | yes |
| **`sign`** | `rpc(key_management::SIGN_REQUEST, …)` (`keys.rs:105`) | **no** |

`rpc` and `rpc_void` both end in `Transport::Tsp { .. } => Err(unsupported_over_tsp(msg_type))` (`client/mod.rs:1140`, `1172`), so a TSP client calling the raw-bytes signing oracle gets `UnsupportedTransport` — while the same client can derive-and-sign perfectly well.

## Everything needed for the fix already exists

- The Trust Task is defined and handled: `spec/vta/keys/sign/1.0` / `TASK_KEYS_SIGN_1_0` (`trust_tasks.rs:301`), handler `handle_sign` (`vta-service/src/trust_tasks/keys.rs:168`), reaching the identical `operations::keys::sign_payload` spine with the same `{ key_id, payload, algorithm }` body and the same base64url conventions.
- The bridge exists and is the documented pattern for exactly this: `rpc_tt` keeps the dedicated REST route while the DIDComm leg dispatches the Trust Task, and its TSP arm notes the surface "needed no per-operation work to reach TSP".

So the change looks like moving `sign()` from `rpc` to `rpc_tt` with `TASK_KEYS_SIGN_1_0`, keeping `POST /keys/{key_id}/sign` as the REST leg — the same shape `derive_and_sign` beside it already has. The three signing paths then behave identically across transports instead of one being the odd one out.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

A consumer that signs through the VTA and is migrating DIDComm → TSP finds that its *one* VTA call is the one that doesn't port. Cierge's gateway is that consumer: signing is the only VTA operation it performs, so `sign()` alone decides whether its sessions are transport-agnostic. It can work around this today by calling `dispatch_trust_task(TASK_KEYS_SIGN_1_0, …)` directly and hand-decoding the payload — but a workaround that re-implements a typed method in every consumer is the argument for fixing it here, not there.

Worth deciding alongside: whether any other `rpc`-routed methods with an existing Trust Task twin should move at the same time (the keys, seeds and ACL slices in `docs/05-design-notes/trust-task-uri-registry.md` all list one), or whether `sign` is pulled forward on its own because it is the operation consumers actually build on.

Related: affinidi/cierge#48, and `docs/design-context-hierarchy.md` in that repo, where the per-domain signing session is specified against the Trust Task for this reason.

title: fix: re-export resolve_vta_with_resolver alongside resolve_vta
body:
Mine to fix — I added the function in #813 and missed the re-export list.

## The gap

`provision_client` re-exports a **curated** list:

```rust
pub use resolve::{ResolvedVta, resolve_vta};
```

#813 added `resolve_vta_with_resolver` to `resolve.rs` without adding it there. The function exists and is `pub`, but not at the path its sibling lives at — `provision_client::resolve_vta` works, `provision_client::resolve_vta_with_resolver` doesn't, and a consumer has to reach through `provision_client::resolve::` instead.

OpenVTC hit exactly that wiring its TSP discovery tests (OpenVTC/openvtc#198) and worked around it with the deeper path. An asymmetric export on a pair of functions differing only by *"and here is the resolver"* is the kind of thing every future caller stubs a toe on.

## The change

One line, plus a compile-only test that imports **both** names from `provision_client` and fails to build if either is pruned from the list again — which is precisely how this was introduced. That felt more useful than a comment asking the next editor to remember.

Additive: the deeper path keeps working, so nothing that already compiles breaks.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --features session,client,didcomm,provision-client` — 462 + 16 + 78 + … all green, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` (CI's invocation) — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `scripts/check-version-bumps.sh` — `ok vta-sdk: 0.20.4 -> 0.20.5`
- `scripts/check-changelogs.sh` — `ok vta-sdk: 0.20.4 -> 0.20.5 (documented)`

Incidentally this also exercised #815 for real: the worktree is under `/tmp`, and both guards reported correctly rather than the vacuous "nothing to check" they'd have given before that fix.

## Follow-on

Once 0.20.5 publishes, OpenVTC can drop its `provision_client::resolve::` workaround and the note explaining it.

title: feat(acl): let an ACL listing say which direction its context filter reads (#822)
body:
Closes #822.

`GET /acl?context=X` answers "who may act **in** X" — entries scoped to X or to an ancestor of it. That is correct, and it is one of *two* questions a context id raises, because a context id names a subtree. The other — "what is granted **beneath** X" — had no way to be asked, and asking it with the act-in filter returns precisely the entries that are **not** the answer: the ancestors keeping their authority, with every leaf-scoped grant omitted. Short, not empty, so it reads as complete.

That bites on revocation. Once sub-contexts exist the least-privilege layout is a leaf per purpose (`<tenant>/<unit>/<purpose>` — partly because, absent a per-key actor grant (#818), a context of its own is the only way to scope a caller to one key), and a sweep of `<tenant>/<unit>` then misses *every* principal under it. Cierge's kill switch hit exactly this (affinidi/cierge#49): a gateway grant at `<domain>/attestation` survived the cut and could keep signing as the killed domain while the report said success.

## The shape

An explicit direction on the filter, defaulting to today's behaviour:

| direction | question | predicate |
|---|---|---|
| `acting-in` (default) | who may act **in** X? | entry scope `is_ancestor_or_self` of X |
| `subtree` | what is granted **beneath** X? | X `is_ancestor_or_self` of the entry scope |
| `any` | whose authority **touches** X's subtree? | either |

One enum rather than a `subtree=true` flag — the issue's own open question. "Either direction" is the third question an auditor actually asks and a boolean cannot spell it. The predicate is the existing one with its arguments swapped (`ActScope::acts_within` beside `covers`), so both directions stay the same pure, store-free segment comparison.

Surfaces: `GET /acl?context=…&direction=…`, a `direction` member on the `spec/vta/acl/list/1.0` payload (and the DIDComm `list-acl` body), `pnm|cnm acl list --direction`, the offline `vta acl list --direction`, and `VtaClient::list_acl_in_direction`. `VtaClient::list_acl` is unchanged and stays `acting-in`; the client omits the parameter entirely at the default, so a request meaning what an older VTA already does still reaches it.

## Two edges, both deliberate and tested

- **An unrestricted (super-admin) entry is *not* in the `subtree` answer.** It names no context, so it is not a grant *of* the branch — it is authority everywhere, which `acting-in` already reports. Returning it would hand a caller revoking a compromised branch its own super-admin to delete. `any` is where an auditor asks for it.
- **An entry naming contexts inside *and* outside the branch *is* in it.** It does hold a grant inside, so omitting it would under-report — the failure mode being fixed. Whether to delete the entry or narrow its scope is then a decision made with the entry in hand.

## Fail-closed

Absent parameter is byte-for-byte the previous behaviour, pinned at the scope, entry, and operation layers. An unparseable direction is refused **with the valid set** rather than defaulted, and a direction with no context is refused rather than silently answered with the whole ACL — guessing which of two opposite questions the caller meant is the defect, one level up. Visibility (`is_acl_entry_auditable`) is still applied before the filter in every direction, pinned by a test that a sibling-unit admin sees nothing under `acme/eng` in any of the three. The CLI prints the question it asked beside the count, including on an empty result — otherwise an empty sweep and a wrong-direction sweep look identical.

## The VTC question, answered rather than done

Its equivalent filter deliberately did **not** follow. The VTC listing is bound to the canonical `acl/list/0.1` Trust Task, whose payload is `additionalProperties: false` over `{cursor, ext, pageSize, role, scope, subjectPrefix}`, so a `direction` member there is an openvtc spec change (or an `ext` member), not a local one — adding it unilaterally would be exactly the canonical-conformance drift the VTC migration exists to remove. Recorded as a follow-up in `docs/05-design-notes/acl-scope-semantics.md`, with the trap for whoever picks it up: the VTC list is **paginated**, so `direction` must also join `ListAclQuery::cursor_binding`, or a resumed sweep silently changes question mid-listing.

## Testing

- `vta-sdk`: mirror/segment-awareness/union/default-equivalence/wire-spelling + refusal of an unknown value on `ContextDirection` and `ActScope::acts_within`.
- `vti-common`: the sweep finds the leaves the act filter omits, stops at the branch (sibling + `acme/engineering` lookalike), does not offer up the super-admin, acts-nowhere is in no direction, default reproduces the old filter entry for entry.
- `vta-service` operations: all three directions over the tenant/unit/purpose layout, visibility not widened, direction-without-context refused.
- `vta-service` REST integration: `?direction=` end to end incl. `acting-in` == absent, a typo answered with the valid set (400), and `?direction=` alone refused.
- `vta-sdk` REST client: the parameter rides the query only when it is not the default.

`cargo fmt` / `clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean; full `vta-service`, `vta-sdk`, `vti-common`, `vta-cli-common`, `pnm-cli`, `cnm-cli` suites green. All three release guards (`check-changelogs.sh`, `check-version-bumps.sh`, `check-lockfile-self-pins.sh`) pass against `origin/main`.

Version bumps: vta-sdk 0.20.5, vti-common 0.11.27, vta-service 0.12.42, vta-cli-common 0.10.16, pnm-cli 0.11.11, cnm-cli 0.11.10.
