title: ACL listing cannot enumerate a subtree, so a revocation sweep by context misses descendants
body:
`GET /acl?context=…` answers "who can act **in** this context", by design. There is no way to ask the complementary question — "who can act **anywhere beneath** this context" — and a consumer sweeping a subtree to revoke it gets a silently incomplete answer.

## The asymmetry

`operations::acl::list_acl` filters on `acl_entry_can_act_in(entry, ctx)` = `entry.act_scope().covers(ctx)` (`vti-common/src/acl/mod.rs:854`). `covers` is `is_ancestor_or_self(scope, ctx)`, so:

| Entry scoped at | `?context=acme/eng` returns it | Correct for "who can act in acme/eng" |
|---|---|---|
| `acme` (ancestor) | yes | yes — folder authority reaches down |
| `acme/eng` (self) | yes | yes |
| `acme/eng/team-a` (descendant) | **no** | yes — it holds no authority over `acme/eng` |

Every row is right for the question the filter asks. The problem is that a second, equally natural question has no way to be asked, and the filter's shape makes the wrong answer look like a complete one — an empty-ish result rather than an error.

## Why it bites: revocation sweeps

Once sub-contexts exist, the natural least-privilege pattern is a leaf per purpose — partly *because* of #818: with no per-key actor grant, a context of its own is the only way to scope a caller to one key. So a tenant lays out `<tenant>/<unit>/<purpose>` and grants each principal its own leaf.

The revocation path then inverts the containment direction. "Revoke everything under `<tenant>/<unit>`" is a sweep over descendants, and `?context=<tenant>/<unit>` returns exactly the entries that are **not** the ones being revoked — the ancestors keeping their authority — while omitting every leaf-scoped grant the sweep exists to cut.

Concretely in Cierge (affinidi/cierge#49, `docs/design-context-hierarchy.md`): its kill switch sweeps a compromised domain's ACLs with this filter (`crates/cierge-orchestrator/src/kill.rs:93`). Under a per-purpose leaf layout, a gateway grant at `<domain>/attestation` survives the cut and can keep signing as the killed domain, while the kill report says it succeeded. Cierge is fixing this on its side by sweeping an enumerated set of leaves, which works because it knows every purpose it creates — but it cannot catch a sub-context created by anything else, and each consumer adopting sub-contexts re-derives the same workaround.

This is the `allowed_contexts.is_empty()` lesson from `acl-scope-semantics.md` in a new place: an ACL question whose answer is only meaningful paired with the direction being asked, and a call site that cannot express which direction it means.

## Suggested shape

An explicit direction on the list filter, defaulting to today's behaviour:

- `GET /acl?context=…` — unchanged: entries that can act *in* the context (ancestor-or-self).
- `GET /acl?context=…&subtree=true` — entries whose act scope is at or **beneath** the context, i.e. `is_ancestor_or_self(ctx, scope)`.

Both are pure segment comparisons over data already in the entry; the primitive exists (`vti_common::context_path`) and the predicate is just the existing one with its arguments swapped. Additive and fail-closed: absent parameter = today's semantics exactly.

Worth deciding alongside it:

- Whether the two are separate flags or one enum, since "either direction" (ancestors *and* descendants) is what an auditor asking "everyone with any authority touching this subtree" actually wants, and is a third question again.
- Whether the same direction problem exists on any other context-filtered surface, and whether the VTC's ancestry-aware `GET /acl?context=…` list filter should follow.

Related: #818 (per-key actor grants — the gap that pushes consumers toward a leaf per key in the first place), #817 / `docs/05-design-notes/multi-tenant-signing.md`, `docs/05-design-notes/hierarchical-contexts.md`, `docs/05-design-notes/acl-scope-semantics.md`.

title: test: assert TSP discovery instead of trusting it
body:
Closes the caveat #196 shipped with. Uses the seam VTI #813 added upstream.

## Why this couldn't be done before

#196 wired trust tasks onto a TSP leg, but `resolve_vta` built its resolver from the environment — so no test could point discovery at a fixture. The enablement path was verified **by construction rather than execution**, which I flagged at the time. vta-sdk 0.20.3 added the injection seam; this uses it.

## Changes

- **Bump vta-sdk 0.20.2 → 0.20.4.** 0.20.3 carries the seam; 0.20.4 adds signing-oracle authorization *documentation* (VTI #805), no behaviour change. Verified rather than assumed — workspace builds and the full suite pass unchanged.

- **Split the decision from its application.** `discover_tsp_mediator` returns a `TspDiscovery` — `Advertised` / `NotAdvertised` / `Unavailable` — and `enable_tsp_with_resolver` applies it. Returned rather than logged-and-dropped so the decision is assertable: the caller turns it into a log line, a test turns it into an assertion. Same shape as the supervisor's `rebuild_due` in #195, for the same reason.

- **`NotAdvertised` and `Unavailable` stay distinct.** Both degrade to DIDComm, but only one is worth an operator's attention, and collapsing them would report "this VTA offers no TSP" about one we merely failed to ask — the false-certainty #187 fixed in the panel (R6.4).

## Tests

Five, seeding a document and asserting what discovery makes of it — in-process, no network, no live VTA:

- the reference deployment's dual `#tsp` + `#vta-didcomm` shape yields its mediator
- a DIDComm-only VTA is `NotAdvertised`
- an unresolvable DID is `Unavailable`
- a `#tsp` entry carrying a URL instead of a mediator DID is not treated as advertised

**The fifth pins something surprising**, found because my first attempt at the third asserted the opposite and failed: an unresolvable `did:web` reports `NotAdvertised`, **not** `Unavailable`. `resolve_vta_endpoint` synthesizes `https://<domain>` from the DID and returns it as REST, so discovery "succeeds". The outcome is right — degrade to DIDComm — but reached by a route that hides the resolution failure, and only `did:web`/`did:webvh` have a domain to synthesize from. Pinned so the next reader doesn't rediscover it the hard way.

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

## One wart, mine

`provision_client/mod.rs` re-exports `resolve_vta` but not `resolve_vta_with_resolver` — an asymmetry I introduced with the function in VTI #813. The module is `pub`, so the deeper path reaches it and that's what this uses, with a note in the code. An upstream re-export fix is worth doing so the canonical path exists; it's a one-line change to that `pub use` list.

## Still not covered

A trust task **actually traversing** TSP end to end. That needs MockVta to speak TSP (`tsp_profile` is `None` in its test app, on latest VTI main too) and is genuinely larger. This closes the discovery half — that everything up to `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` does the right thing against a real document — which was the part that was assumed rather than tested.

title: test(vtc): close the unpublished Trust Task manifest backlog (#709)
body:
Closes #709.

## What #709 asked for

Twenty task URIs the VTC router enforced were absent from
`trust-tasks/index.json`, parked in the census test's `UNPUBLISHED_OK` table.
The issue's own completion criterion: *"As each family is published, delete its
row from `UNPUBLISHED_OK`. When the table is empty, this issue is done."*

## What actually resolved it

Not twenty specs authored into that manifest — the **#710 migration**. Every
one of the twenty now binds a canonical `https://trusttasks.org/spec/vtc/<slug>`
URI published by the upstream registry, verified against `trust_tasks_rs` by
`every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry`. Measured across all four binding
sites (`vtc-service/src`, `vta-sdk/src`, `cnm-cli/src`,
`vtc-service/admin-ui/src`), **zero** of the twenty still touch the old
authority. The rows were dead exceptions holding a closed backlog open.

The table stays in place, empty. The assertion behind it is still load-bearing:
a new `openvtc/vtc/` binding with no manifest row fails rather than silently
reopening the backlog.

## The manifest's description was false

It claimed to be the *"source of truth for trusttasks.org publication"* with
*"CI publishes Draft entries on every merge to main per spec §9.4"*. No CI job
has ever read `trust-tasks/index.json` — that pipeline was never built, which
#709 itself flagged. The description now records what the file is: a historical
record of the retired `openvtc/vtc` authority, 60 entries retired and 6 awaiting
a canonical fold.

## The five `credential-exchange` directories

#709 also asked whether these were *"published or deleted"*, describing them as
in neither the manifest nor any binding. **That is no longer true and they
should not be deleted.** They carry conformant public-registry IDs
(`https://trusttasks.org/spec/credential-exchange/<verb>/1.0`) and are bound
live by `vta_sdk::protocols::credential_exchange`. They are absent from *this*
manifest correctly — it is scoped `org: openvtc, domain: vtc`, and these are
cross-domain canonical slugs that belong upstream. Follow-up filed separately;
nothing to change here.

## Verification

All 7 census tests pass:

```
test manifest_status_vocabulary_matches_spec ... ok
test every_manifest_entry_has_files_on_disk ... ok
test every_bound_vtc_task_exists_in_the_registry ... ok
test no_new_bindings_on_the_retired_authority ... ok
test every_bound_task_is_published_or_excepted ... ok
test retired_tasks_are_not_bound ... ok
test every_published_task_is_bound_or_excepted ... ok
```

No crate source changed (tests/ and workspace-root JSON only), so no version
bump — `check-version-bumps.sh` excludes `tests/` by convention.

title: VTC Trust Tasks: 20 bound tasks are absent from the published manifest
body:
Split out of #537's manifest-drift follow-up. Pinned by the census added alongside this issue (`vtc-service/tests/trust_task_manifest.rs`), which currently carries them in an `UNPUBLISHED_OK` exception table so the backlog cannot grow silently.

## The gap

`trust-tasks/index.json` self-describes as the source of truth for trusttasks.org publication. Whole feature families shipped after it was last reconciled and were never added. The router enforces these task URIs; the manifest publishes none of them:

| Family | Tasks |
|---|---|
| Backup | `backup/export/1.0`, `backup/import/1.0` |
| Admin invites | `admin/invites/manage/1.0`, `admin/invites/revoke/1.0` |
| Invitations | `invitations/issue/1.0`, `invitations/revoke/1.0` |
| Members | `members/purge/1.0`, `members/removed/1.0`, `members/request-vmc/1.0`, `members/self-remove-receipt/1.0`, `spec/members/request-vmc/1.0`, `spec/members/vmc/1.0` |
| Auth | `auth/admin-session/1.0`, `auth/recognise/challenge/1.0` |
| Other | `directory/query/1.0`, `ceremonies/list/1.0`, `recognition/check/1.0`, `relationships/graph/1.0`, `spec/join-requests/submit-receipt/1.0` |

Plus five task directories on disk (`trust-tasks/credential-exchange/{issue,offer,present,query,request}/1.0`) that are in neither the manifest nor any binding — decide whether those are published or deleted.

## Work

Each entry needs a manifest row **and** `spec.md` + `schema.json` on disk — the census test `every_manifest_entry_has_files_on_disk` enforces the second half, so a manifest-only addition fails.

As each family is published, delete its row from `UNPUBLISHED_OK`. When the table is empty, this issue is done.

## Note on urgency

Lower than it first appears: no CI workflow currently reads `trust-tasks/index.json`, so the "CI publishes Draft entries on every merge to main" claim in the manifest's own `description` field is aspirational. Nothing is actually being published today. That is worth either building or removing from the description — and it is the reason this is a backlog item rather than a live consumer-facing defect.

Depends on the URI-shape question in the companion issue: if the authority/path shape changes, every one of these should be published in the corrected form rather than added twice.

title: fix(vta-service): Nitro enclave attestation + did:webvh persistence
body:
## Summary

Fixes required to run the VTA signing service inside an AWS Nitro Enclave, plus
`did:webvh` log-persistence correctness fixes so a service keeps its identity
across restarts.

## Changes

**Enclave attestation**
- Fix the NSM ioctl request encoding: the length field passed to the Nitro
  Security Module ioctl must be a `u64`, not a `u32`. The wrong width corrupted
  the request struct on aarch64 and caused attestation calls to fail.

**did:webvh persistence**
- Persist the auto-generated `did:webvh` log to the webvh keyspace so the DID
  document history survives restarts.
- Persist the auto-generated `did:webvh` record and backfill it on restore, so a
  restored instance keeps its identity.
- Resolve the service's own DID via the network-mode resolver during the first
  enable handshake, instead of a resolver path that isn't available at that point.

**Deploy / build**
- Exclude signing keys and enclave runtime state from the Docker build context.
- Restore per-crate `COPY` layering + the full workspace manifest list for better
  build-cache reuse.

## Testing

Built and run inside the enclave: attestation succeeds and the DID persists
across restarts.

title: Confirm (and document) per-key access enforcement on key-management/sign
body:
Small, but a security decision elsewhere rests on it.

## The claim being relied on

`SignRequestBody.key_id` is documented in vta-sdk as *"Key ID to sign with (must be an active key the caller has access to)"*, and `KeyRecord` carries a `context_id`. Taken together that implies the VTA **refuses a sign request for a key the caller does not hold**, and that keys are scoped per context.

## Why it matters

A companion proposal (V1: have the VTA *issue* attestations rather than blind-sign supplied bytes, setting `sub` from the caller's authorized domain) was **declined on 2026-07-26**, partly on the reasoning that the identity property is already available: scope a multi-domain caller's capability to exactly the key ids it should sign with, and it cannot sign as another domain even though the VTA does not inspect the payload.

That reasoning is sound **only if the service actually enforces per-key access**. I read it off the SDK's API contract, not from observing the service — so it is an assumption, and a load-bearing one. Cierge's gateway now signs as multiple domains through one VTA session (affinidi/cierge#41), which is exactly the configuration where this matters.

## Ask

1. Confirm the service enforces it: a caller requesting `sign` for a `key_id` outside its ACL scope is refused, not served.
2. If it does, document it as a guarantee rather than an aside in a field comment — callers are making authorization decisions on it.
3. If it does **not**, say so here: V1 stops being optional, since without either mechanism a compromised multi-domain signer can sign as any domain it can name.

## Related

- affinidi/cierge#44 — the attestation gap this sits under.
- The declined V1 also covered timestamp and claim-shape control (backdating, TTL extension), which per-key scoping does **not** address. That residual stands regardless of the answer here.

title: ACL grants cannot scope a caller to specific key ids (only to a whole context)
body:
Split out of the design review in #817 (`docs/05-design-notes/multi-tenant-signing.md`, R2). Stands on its own merits — this is a least-privilege gap independent of the Cierge deployment that surfaced it.

## The gap

The **resource** dimension of an ACL grant is expressible only as a *context*.

`AclEntry.capabilities` is a flat `Vec<Capability>`, and `Capability::Sign` is unparameterized (`vti-common/src/acl/mod.rs:122-145`). So this cannot be said:

> this caller may invoke the signing oracle on **exactly key K**

The only way to scope a caller to one key today is to give that key **a context of its own**. That works — it is what the design note recommends for multi-tenant signers — but it forces context topology to encode per-key authorization, which is a different concern. Any consumer that legitimately needs one key out of a shared context must be handed the whole context.

## Why `signable_keys` is not the answer

`ContextPolicy.signable_keys` (`vta-sdk/src/context_policy.rs:48-50`) already restricts which key ids the signing oracle may be invoked on — but it is **resource-bound by design**: it constrains the key's context for *every* actor uniformly, including super-admin. That property is load-bearing (it is what lets a VTC- or fleet-pushed policy bind every signer, relaxable only through policy CRUD).

It therefore cannot express "*this caller*, this key". The two mechanisms are complementary, not substitutes — this issue asks for the actor-scoped half.

## Proposal

An optional actor-scoped key filter on the ACL entry, **intersected with** — never widening — the existing context scope:

```rust
/// Key ids this entry may invoke the signing oracle on. `None` = every key
/// in `allowed_contexts` (today's behaviour). Intersects with the context
/// scope; it can only narrow, never widen, so an entry naming a key outside
/// its contexts still cannot use it.
#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
pub allowed_keys: Option<BTreeSet<String>>,
```

Enforced in `operations::keys::sign_payload` as a fourth gate, **after** the existing `auth.require_context(ctx)` (`vta-service/src/operations/keys.rs:840`) so a caller can never reach a key outside its contexts by naming it here.

Additive and fail-closed: `None` on every existing row preserves behaviour byte-identically, the same way `capabilities` was introduced.

## Why a separate field rather than parameterising `Capability::Sign`

`Capability::Sign { keys: … }` would change the shape of a serialized enum that already ships in ACL rows and on the `acl_management` wire. A sibling `Option` field is additive and needs no migration. (Open to the alternative if someone prefers it, but the migration cost looks disproportionate.)

## Scope of the change

- `vti-common/src/acl/mod.rs` — the field, plus an accessor that returns the effective decision rather than exposing the raw `Option` (see the `ActScope` precedent below).
- `vta-service/src/operations/keys.rs` — gate 4 in `sign_payload`. Note all three transports (REST, DIDComm `key-management/1.0/sign-request`, `keys/sign` Trust Task) funnel through that one function, so this is one edit, not three.
- `vta-sdk/src/protocols/acl_management/{create,update}.rs` — wire plumbing.
- `vta-cli-common` — an `--allowed-keys` flag on `acl create` / `acl update`.
- Docs: `docs/02-vta/integration-guide.md` §"What authorizes a sign request" gains gate 4.

## Traps worth stating up front

1. **Do not add a bare `is_empty()` check.** `allowed_contexts` already has the empty-means-two-different-things problem that `ActScope` exists to solve (see `docs/05-design-notes/acl-scope-semantics.md` — it has produced three separate defects: #746, #770, #769). `Some(empty_set)` must mean **authorized on no keys**, not "unrestricted"; `None` means unrestricted. Model it so the distinction cannot be got backwards, and do not test emptiness at call sites.
2. **Casing drift on the wire.** `CreateAclBody` is the exact struct where a camelCase/snake_case mismatch once let an empty `allowed_contexts` silently mint a super-admin (#656/#658). Whatever `allowed_keys` serializes as, pin it with a round-trip test and keep `deny_unknown_fields` behaviour consistent with its siblings.
3. **Revocation semantics.** Narrowing an entry's `allowed_keys` should behave like any other privilege reduction — check whether the existing session-revocation path on reduction (`is_privilege_reduction`) needs to account for it, or a caller keeps the wider set until its access token expires.

## Explicitly out of scope

This does **not** address the threat in #805 — a process that legitimately signs for N identities holds authority for N identities, and no authorization refinement changes that (#817, Finding 2). This is about being able to express least privilege where the split *is* meaningful.

title: docs: design review of multi-tenant signing (#805)
body:
Design review requested off the back of #805. Docs-only — no code changes, no version bumps.

Adds `docs/05-design-notes/multi-tenant-signing.md`, written after reading the VTA's authorization path and the Cierge gateway that motivated the question.

## The finding that reframes the issue

#805 asked whether the VTA enforces per-key access on sign. **It does** — three gates, confirmed and pinned in #814. But reviewing what that buys turned up something more important:

**Authorization cannot solve the threat #805 states.**

A process that legitimately signs for N identities *holds authority for N identities*. Every gate sits downstream of that credential, and none can distinguish "the gateway signing for domain A because a domain-A request arrived" from "the gateway signing for domain A because it was compromised" — the decision that a request belongs to a tenant is made **inside** the process, before the VTA is called.

So no refinement of the VTA's model fixes it. Not per-key grants, not tighter policy, not V1. Only two things do: don't give one process that credential, or require a factor the attacker cannot supply (consent / out-of-band ratification — which the VTA has, and which are wrong per-request on a gateway attesting every proxied call).

## The VTA is already right; Cierge is a costed deviation

One principal = one DID = one context = one process, consistently: `provision_integration` gives each integration its own DID + ACL + context; `vta-mcp` documents itself as "a dedicated, context-scoped vta-mcp (the agent's ACL bounds it to its context)"; the agents guide provisions a context per agent.

The Cierge gateway shares one session across every domain — and is honest about it. Its threat model says the fix yields "the ability to **request** signatures while it lasts… revocable by **one** ACL entry", and §10.7 states cross-domain separation there is "only as strong as one process boundary". Nobody overclaimed. The gap is that **#805's declined-V1 reasoning assumed a property that deployment's shape does not provide.**

**Why the deviation happened is the thing worth fixing.** The gateway signs over DIDComm, so a session costs a mediator websocket per DID — and the mediator permits one per DID (the `duplicate-channel` constraint #810 hit). The correct pattern was expensive, so a consumer took the cheap one.

Signing doesn't need DIDComm. Over REST a session is a bearer token, so per-tenant sessions cost N JWTs and the websocket ceiling disappears. **Lower the cost and the correct pattern becomes the easy one** — that's the lever.

## Recommendations

| | Solves the threat | Effort | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| **R1a** per-domain REST sessions | Partly — everything short of credential theft | Low | Cierge |
| **R1b** signer sidecar per domain | Yes | Medium | Cierge |
| **R2** `allowed_keys` actor grants | No — fixes a *different*, real gap | Low | VTA |
| **R3** token attenuation | Enables R1b cheaply | Medium | VTA, when a 2nd consumer appears |
| **R4** document the rule | No — prevents recurrence | Trivial | VTA |

**R2 is worth flagging on its own merits.** `AclEntry.capabilities` is a flat `Vec<Capability>` and `Capability::Sign` is unparameterized, so "this caller may sign with exactly key K" cannot be expressed — the only way to scope a caller to one key is to give that key its own context. That's a genuine least-privilege gap independent of Cierge. `signable_keys` is *not* the answer and the note says so: it's resource-bound by design, constraining the key's context for every actor uniformly.

**R3 is deliberately deferred.** The note argues against building attenuation for one consumer — R1a solves Cierge; build the general primitive when a second consumer proves the shape, so two real call sites drive it instead of one hypothetical.

## What it explicitly does not argue

**Not a case for reopening V1.** V1 was declined partly on per-key scoping, and this review shows per-key scoping doesn't deliver for a shared signer — but V1 fails the same Finding-2 test, since a compromised process authenticated as a multi-domain principal would simply have the VTA issue the attestation it asks for. The residual V1 *did* address — timestamp and claim-shape control — is untouched and stands on its own merits.

## Verification

Every quoted claim checked against the tree rather than memory: the `vta-mcp` and Cierge comments quoted verbatim with line numbers, `Capability::Sign`'s shape, the absence of any attenuation/exchange endpoint, the REST sign route, and the one-websocket-per-DID mediator constraint (CHANGELOG:217).

title: fix(ci): stop the release guards passing vacuously from a symlinked path
body:
Found while working on #813, where both guards told me "nothing to check" on a PR that definitely changed crate source.

## The bug

`check-version-bumps.sh` and `check-changelogs.sh` strip `$ROOT/` from the manifest paths `cargo metadata` reports, to attribute each changed file to its crate. `ROOT` came from `pwd`, which **preserves** symlinks; `cargo metadata` reports the **physical** path.

On macOS a git worktree under `/tmp` (a symlink to `/private/tmp`) makes the two disagree. The prefix never matches, every crate dir stays absolute, every changed file fails attribution, and the script reports *"No publishable-crate source changed — nothing to check"* and **exits 0**.

Reproduced on `64497b5b` — an unbumped edit to `vta-sdk/src/vp.rs`:

```
/private/tmp/vti-guard-fix -> exit 1   ← correctly fails
/tmp/vti-guard-fix         -> exit 0   ← silently passes
```

Same commit, same guard, opposite answers.

**CI is not affected** — it checks out a normal path. But anyone using a `/tmp` worktree gets a green guard that checked nothing, which is worse than no guard, because it reads as confirmation.

## The fix

- **`pwd -P`** so `ROOT` is the physical path `cargo metadata` reports. Applied to `check-lockfile-self-pins.sh` too: it doesn't strip paths today so it was unaffected, but it derives `ROOT` the same way and shouldn't acquire the bug later.

- **A guard-the-guard** in both attributing scripts: if any crate dir is still absolute after the strip, exit 2 rather than continue. `pwd -P` closes the cause known today; this closes the *class*. The failure mode being fixed is **silence**, so the fix should not depend on having anticipated every way the prefix can mismatch.

## Verification

- From the previously-broken `/tmp` path, the version-bump guard now **exits 1** on an unbumped source change (was 0). Both paths agree.
- All three guards still **exit 0 on a clean tree** from both paths — no false positives.
- The assertion was exercised directly against crafted input: fires on absolute dirs, passes relative ones. An untested error path is how you get a guard that doesn't guard.
- This PR touches only `scripts/`, so the guards correctly report "nothing to check" — and since a *vacuous* pass would now exit 2, exit 0 confirms it's a genuine one. The fix validates itself.

No shell linter in CI and `shellcheck` isn't available locally, so the scripts were checked with `bash -n` only.

title: docs(vta): make the signing oracle's authorization model a guarantee (#805)
body:
Answers #805.

## The question

`SignRequestBody.key_id` was documented as *"must be an active key the caller has access to"*. A companion proposal (have the VTA issue attestations rather than blind-sign supplied bytes) was **declined** partly because per-key scoping was thought to already deliver the identity property. But that was read off the SDK's API contract, not observed in the service — and Cierge's gateway now signs as multiple domains through one VTA session, which is exactly where it matters.

## The answer: yes, enforced — and more strictly than the comment implied

`operations::keys::sign_payload` (`vta-service/src/operations/keys.rs:839-861`) applies three gates:

1. **The caller's context scope** — `auth.require_context(ctx)?` on the key's `context_id`, routed through `ActScope` (the guard `CLAUDE.md` flags as the one people get backwards, so it is the right mechanism rather than an ad-hoc `is_empty()` check).
2. **The key's context policy** — `signable_keys` is *resource-bound*: it constrains the key's context **regardless of the actor, including a super-admin**. That is what lets a fleet- or VTC-pushed policy bind every signer; the owner relaxes it via policy CRUD, never by holding a bigger role.
3. **Unscoped keys are super-admin only** — a key with no `context_id` has no context and therefore no policy to constrain it, so the role floor is the only guardrail left.

All three transports — REST `POST /keys/{key_id}/sign`, DIDComm `key-management/1.0/sign-request`, and the `keys/sign` Trust Task — funnel through that single function. One enforcement point, not three.

**So the reasoning that declined V1 holds.** Scope a multi-domain caller to specific keys and it cannot sign as a domain it does not hold.

## The caveat worth knowing (issue ask #2)

**Enforcement is per *context*, not per *key id*.** Holding a context authorizes **every** key in it.

A signer acting for several identities therefore needs **a context each**. Putting several domains' keys in one context and scoping the caller to that context authorizes all of them — and nothing about the resulting sign request would look wrong. `signable_keys` (gate 2) does give per-key narrowing, but it is opt-in policy an operator must write; it is not the default.

That distinction was stated nowhere, and it is precisely the misconfiguration that would silently void the guarantee. It is now documented.

## What changed

- **`docs/02-vta/integration-guide.md`** — new §"What authorizes a sign request": the three gates, the all-transports note, and the per-context caveat called out as a block quote. Best-practice item 3 links to it.
- **`vta-sdk/src/protocols/key_management/sign.rs`** — the field comment now states the guarantee and points at the doc, instead of implying it in passing.
- **Two regression tests**, because two of the three layers had none — and they were the two the declined proposal actually rests on:
  - `sign_payload_refuses_a_key_outside_the_callers_contexts` (gate 1)
  - `sign_payload_restricts_unscoped_keys_to_super_admin` (gate 3)

  Gate 2 was already covered by `sign_payload_honours_context_policy_signable_keys`.

## On the tests being real

Both new tests were verified by removing the check they pin and confirming they fail.

Worth recording: **my first attempt at that verification was wrong.** `auth.require_context(ctx)?;` appears seven times in the file, so a `replace(..., 1)` mutation hit a different function entirely — the check under test was untouched and the test passed, which I nearly read as "defence in depth" rather than "bad mutation". Redoing it by line number showed the test does fail. Anyone re-verifying should mutate by line, not by string.

## Verification

- `vta-service` lib: 685 tests pass, 0 fail.
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` (CI's exact command) clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.
- `vta-sdk` patch bump 0.20.2 → 0.20.3 keeps the `[patch.crates-io]` self-pin valid (a *minor* bump is what breaks it).

## Residual, unaddressed

The declined V1 also covered timestamp and claim-shape control (backdating, TTL extension). Per-key scoping does not address that, and this PR does not change it — that residual stands.

title: feat: let a caller supply the resolver for VTA transport discovery
body:
Closes the testability half of what OpenVTC/openvtc#185 needed. Additive; no signature changes.

## The problem

`resolve_vta_endpoint` builds its `DIDCacheClient` from the environment, so a consumer has **no way to point discovery at a fixture**: seeding a document into its own cache does nothing, because the function never sees that cache.

The practical effect is that *"does this VTA advertise `#tsp`"* — the question #765 and #810 made answerable — can still only be **asserted** against a live deployment. OpenVTC hit this covering its TSP-enablement path and had to leave the assertion unmade, with the wiring verified by construction rather than execution.

## This started as a MockVta fixture, which was the wrong layer

The obvious fix looked like "give `MockVta` a TSP-advertising variant". It cannot work: `preseed_did_docs` seeds the **VTA's own** resolver, and an external consumer resolves through its own. No fixture on the VTA side can reach a consumer's discovery call while that call constructs its resolver internally.

The blocker was never the fixture. It was the missing seam.

## The change

- **`resolve_vta_endpoint_with_resolver(vta_did, &DIDCacheClient)`** and **`provision_client::resolve_vta_with_resolver(...)`** run the same discovery over a caller-supplied resolver. The env-configured entry points delegate to them, so behaviour is unchanged and no caller has to move.
- Follows the pattern **`resolve_mediator_did_with_resolver` already set in the same module**, for the same two reasons: reuse (no second cache per resolve) and testability.
- `provision_client`'s two entry points now share one `flatten`, so they cannot disagree about what an endpoint shape means — the split that keeps "what is advertised" separate from "what we connected over".

## Tests — the assertions that were previously impossible

Four, seeding a document and asserting what discovery makes of it, in-process with no network:

- a dual `#tsp` + `#vta-didcomm` VTA (**the reference deployment's shape**) reports both, in preference order
- a DIDComm-only VTA reports no TSP
- a TSP-only VTA does **not** fall back to a REST URL synthesized from its own domain — the bug `resolve_vta_endpoint`'s own doc calls out, now covered
- a `#tsp` entry carrying a URL instead of a mediator DID is ignored rather than routed through

## Verification

- `cargo test -p vta-sdk --features session,client,didcomm,provision-client` — 462 + 16 + 78 + … all green, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` (CI's invocation) — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `scripts/check-version-bumps.sh` — `ok vta-sdk: 0.20.2 -> 0.20.3`
- `scripts/check-changelogs.sh` — `ok vta-sdk: 0.20.2 -> 0.20.3 (documented)`

## Two things flagged, not fixed

**Pre-existing clippy errors.** `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk --features session,client,didcomm,provision-client --all-targets` reports 3 errors (`didcomm_session.rs:673` "this loop never actually loops", and two others). **Same count on a clean `origin/main`**, none in files this change touches, and CI's own invocation is clean — so unrelated to this PR, but worth someone's attention since that feature combination is what consumers build with.

**A guard blind spot.** Both release guards resolve `$ROOT` via `pwd`, while `cargo metadata` reports the symlink-resolved path. On macOS, running from a worktree under `/tmp` (→ `/private/tmp`) makes the paths mismatch, every crate fails attribution, and both guards **pass vacuously** with "nothing to check". They behave correctly from the canonical path, and CI checks out normally so it is unaffected — but a guard that silently passes when it cannot attribute anything is worth hardening, given these exist precisely to catch what authors forget.

title: refactor(vtc): de-list the raw-byte website tasks
body:
Cleanup, and the only Trust Task backlog item that *removes* surface rather than adding it.

## What

Three endpoints on the website management surface move **file bytes**:

- `GET /v1/website/files/{path}`
- `PUT /v1/website/files/{path}`
- `POST /v1/website/deploy`

A Trust Task's payload is a JSON document, so none of them can be one — there is no document shape for "here are 4 MiB of PNG", and no canonical spec will ever supersede them.

All three were nevertheless gated on a `Trust-Task` header, sharing `openvtc/vtc/website/files/show/1.0` (or `…/deploy/1.0`) — tasks that existed only to give the mount *a* header to check. Because the whole `/website/files/{*path}` mount shared one gate, the `PUT` **and** the `DELETE` both announced themselves as a **read**.

| Endpoint | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /website/files/{path}` | `…/files/show/1.0` | **none** — de-listed |
| `PUT /website/files/{path}` | `…/files/show/1.0` | **none** — de-listed |
| `POST /website/deploy` | `…/deploy/1.0` | **none** — de-listed |
| `DELETE /website/files/{path}` | `…/files/show/1.0` | `spec/vtc/website/files/delete/0.1` |

`DELETE` carries a path, not a payload, so it is a genuine Trust Task — it now binds the canonical task it should have had all along, and is the last of the four canonical website tasks to be wired.

Also: `openvtc/vtc/website/files/delete/1.0` moves `draft` → `retired` with a `supersededBy`, the de-listed specs leave `trust-tasks/`, and the on-disk spec tree now matches the manifest exactly.

**De-listing removes a header check, never `AdminAuth`.** Every one of these endpoints still requires an admin bearer token or session cookie, and the new suite asserts exactly that.

## Effect on the backlog

The retired `openvtc/vtc/` authority drops from **6 bound URIs to 4**, and three census exception rows go away (one of which — `website/files/write/1.0` in `UNBOUND_OK` — was stale: it named a manifest entry that no longer existed).

The remaining four are all genuinely blocked on other work, so this closes out the part of #710 that was actionable:

- `admin/config/{export,import}` — blocked on `communityProfile` moving to `ext` (structural).
- `auth/admin-login` — needs the cookie side-effect moved to a binding/`ext`.
- `config/legacy/manage` — needs a field-ownership audit before its route can go (see below).

## Two things worth a reviewer's eye

**The mount split relies on axum merging same-path method routers per verb.** `/website/files/{*path}` is now two `.route()` calls on one path. If that assumption were wrong it panics at router construction, so `the_split_file_mount_builds` pins it rather than leaving it implicit.

**The tests assert on the error discriminator, not the status.** A re-added gate answers `TrustTaskMissing`, which is a **400** — and these handlers have legitimate 400s of their own (malformed bundle, bad path). My first draft asserted `!= 415` and passed straight through a deliberately reintroduced gate. It now checks the `error` field, and I verified it fails when the gate is put back.

## Upgrade notes

API clients should stop sending a `Trust-Task` header on the three exempt endpoints (a stale one is now ignored there rather than checked). On `DELETE`, send `spec/vtc/website/files/delete/0.1` — the old `…/files/show/1.0` now fails with `TrustTaskMismatch` (415).

Nothing in-tree calls these: the admin SPA, `cnm-cli` and `vta-sdk` are all clear, so no client changes were needed. Documented in `docs/03-vtc/website-and-admin.md`.

## Verification

- `vtc-service`: 1131 tests pass, 0 fail (run **with** the real admin-UI build).
- New `vtc-service/tests/website_task_gating.rs` — 4 tests, mutation-checked by re-adding the gate.
- `cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings` (CI's exact command) clean; `cargo fmt --check` clean.

### Unrelated pre-existing finding

`cargo clippy --all-targets` reports `never_loop` at `vta-sdk/src/didcomm_session.rs:673`, on `main` as well as here — I have not touched that crate. It is **not** a functional bug: the loop's only `continue` sits behind `#[cfg(feature = "tsp")]`, so the lint fires only in the configuration where that arm is compiled out. CI misses it because its clippy job omits `--all-targets`. Flagging, not fixing.

title: feat(vtc)!: step-up means recent, and admin promotion uses it
body:
Two commits: an additive one that makes step-up mean *recent*, and a breaking
one that folds `promote-to-admin` onto the canonical role-change task and
deletes the fused endpoints.

## 1. `acr` cannot express freshness — `Session.acr_expires_at` can (`69b99c5c`)

`StepUpAuth` gated on `acr == "aal2"` and nothing else. That records the
assurance level a session *reached*, not when: a passkey sign-in is `aal2` from
its very first request and `/auth/refresh` preserves it for the session's whole
life. Any route behind that gate would have accepted a sign-in from an hour ago,
losing the property such routes exist for — that a stolen session cannot, by
itself, authorise the next privileged operation.

Freshness already had a home. `Session.acr_expires_at` is stamped by the VTA's
step-up ceremony and honoured by the intrinsic-sender (DIDComm/TSP) resolver,
and its own doc named the missing half: *"a later phase wires REST into the same
read-time downgrade."* This is that phase. It needed **no new JWT claim** — the
`AuthClaims` extractor already loads the session row for the `jti` pin.

- `StepUpAuth` now requires a **live elevation window** as well as `aal2`. An
  absent deadline is refused, not waved through.
- `AuthClaims::require_fresh_step_up(sessions)` applies the identical rule
  in-handler, for routes where only one field value needs it. Both go through
  one `check_fresh_step_up`, so they cannot drift.
- REST deliberately does **not** copy the intrinsic path's read-time `acr`
  rewrite: rewriting would downgrade a passkey-login session *below* the level
  it logged in at. The gate reads the deadline directly, so a stale `acr` can
  never satisfy it and there is nothing to rewrite.

`StepUpAuth` had zero call sites before this, so nothing regresses.

### `purpose: stepUp` is now actually implemented

A comment in `routes/mod.rs` claimed the passkey-login payload's `purpose` field
already selected between login and step-up. No handler read it. The VTC pair
moves to `spec/auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2` (the camelCase `stepUp`
enum; the 0.1 constants in `vta-sdk` were already `#[deprecated]`).

A step-up is not a login with a flag:

| | `purpose: login` | `purpose: stepUp` |
|---|---|---|
| Caller | unauthenticated — the ceremony *is* the auth | must already hold the session |
| Credentials challenged | every registered passkey (discoverable) | **only the caller's own** |
| User verification | as the authenticator offers | **required** — a silent assertion is one factor |
| Result | new session + tokens | existing session elevated in place, **no** tokens |

The ceremony is bound at `start` to the session that asked for it, and
re-checked at `finish` against **both** the session id and its subject. Neither
of `start`'s arrangements is load-bearing alone: `allowCredentials` is a
client-side hint the browser may ignore, and the token presented at `finish`
need not be the one presented at `start`. Without the subject re-check, any
enrolled admin's passkey would elevate anyone's session.

`subject` is honoured rather than noted — it narrows a login challenge, and a
step-up naming anyone but the authenticated subject is refused.

## 2. Breaking — `promote-to-admin` folds onto `members/update` (`e1e4e33a`)

`POST /v1/members/{did}/promote-to-admin/{start,finish}` is **removed**.
Promotion is `PATCH /v1/members/{did}` with `{"role": "admin"}`
(`spec/vtc/members/update/0.1`) on a session carrying a live elevation.

The fused endpoint bundled a WebAuthn UV *ceremony* with a role-change
*operation*: one URI carrying two tasks' worth of semantics, a second
implementation of passkey UV alongside `auth/passkey/login`, and a proof of user
presence that could authorise exactly one operation and nothing else.

Every security property carried over — UV required, the caller's own passkey,
self-promotion refused, serialised under `PROMOTE_LOCK`, the already-admin
re-check inside the critical section, and still routed through
`role_change_via_pipeline(step_up = true)` so `role_change.rego` governs it
(P0.14). What changed is *when* the UV happens: recently, in its own request,
which is what makes the window mean anything.

Two deliberate differences, both called out in the changelog and the retired
spec:

- **The authorising credential id** moved off `AdminPromoted` onto a new
  `AuthSteppedUp` audit event emitted by the ceremony itself. `AdminPromoted`
  gains `authorisingSessionId`, which joins the two rows — an API split needs
  two linked records. Both new fields are `#[serde(default)]`, so archived
  envelopes from either side of the fold still deserialise.
- **Promoting an existing admin is a `200` no-op**, not a `409`. `POST
  …/promote-to-admin` was imperative and promoting an existing admin is
  meaningless; `PATCH` is declarative — the role *should be* admin, and it
  already is — so a retried request is safe. The `409` that mattered still
  guards the concurrent-promotion race.

### The recorded fold target did not hold

The plan for this fold named `acl/change-role` as the destination. That task is
bound to `PATCH /v1/acl/{did}` — a bare ACL write that never runs
`role_change.rego` and serves non-member ACL rows (integrations, install DIDs).
Routing admin promotion through it would have reintroduced the P0.14 policy
bypass the same plan said to preserve. `spec/vtc/members/update/0.1` already ran
the role-change ceremony, and already refused `role=admin` with a message
pointing at the endpoint being deleted. Confirmed with the author before
switching.

`openvtc/vtc/members/promote-to-admin/1.0` is `retired` with a `supersededBy`
and leaves `AWAITING_CANONICAL_FOLD`, which is down to four entries.

## Upgrade notes

The Trust-Task header is matched **exactly**, and the admin SPA is compiled into
the binary, so daemon and SPA move together. External clients do not:

- callers of `POST /v1/members/{did}/promote-to-admin/{start,finish}` must move
  to the step-up + `PATCH` pair;
- callers sending `spec/auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.1` headers to the
  VTC must move to `/0.2`.

There is no grace period on either — the header gate is exact-match.

## Verification

- `vti-common` 348 lib tests, `vtc-service` 692 lib + every integration suite,
  green.
- New: `vtc-service/tests/passkey_step_up.rs` (8), `vti-common` extractor +
  session-window unit tests, rewritten promotion coverage in
  `tests/members_crud.rs`.
- `cargo clippy --all-targets` clean, `cargo fmt --check` clean, admin-UI
  `tsc --noEmit` clean.
- Run `vtc-service` tests **without** `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` — that flag
  leaves the embedded UI dir empty and four `admin_ui::tests` fail on it.

title: feat: evaluate a verifier's DCQL query into a consent summary
body:
First slice of D4, and a correction to how it was scoped. Core logic only — no wiring yet.

## The scoping doc pointed at the wrong path

It recommended manifest-first: fetch `join-requests/manifest`, build a VP, submit it in `JoinRequestSubmitBody.vp`. Reading what the VTC actually serves says otherwise — there are **two** join-VP paths and only one verifies:

| Path | Verification |
|---|---|
| `submit.rs` | `vp` is **opaque JSON**; `presentation.verified` rests on a route-layer hex signature |
| `present.rs` | **Cryptographically verified** — `verify_vp_token`, holder DI proof bound to the verifier's nonce + audience |

`present.rs` draws the contrast itself. So a real presentation in the submit slot would be correct work with **no security value**. The verified path is `credential-exchange` query/present, and the **VTC drives it** — it issues a single-use challenge and a DCQL query built from a registered Accepts criterion. Our role is responder, which is why you scoped it that way.

That also shrinks D4: the doc called a DCQL evaluator "D4's core deliverable" and noted none existed. vta-sdk 0.20.2 now ships `vp.rs` (VTI #437, closed), and D4.1 (manifest discovery) drops out entirely.

## What's here

- **`held_credentials`** — gathers what a persona could present (community-issued credentials + received VRCs), with ids naming their origin (`community:<kind>`, `vrc:<id>`) so a wrong selection is diagnosable from the summary alone.
- **`evaluate_query`** — runs the DCQL match, returns a `DisclosureRequest`: verifier, stated purpose, and every credential answering would reveal. Signs nothing, sends nothing.
- **`present`** — consumes that request **by value**, produces the signed `vp_token`.

**The consent gate is the module's shape, not a flag.** There is no path to a `vp_token` that doesn't first produce the summary a human is shown, and consuming the request by value means an approval can't be replayed against a later challenge.

## One deliberate omission worth reviewing

**No "requested claims" in the summary.** The DCQL match carries the paths the verifier asked for — but `eddsa-jcs-2022` credentials cannot be redacted, so the credential is presented **whole** regardless. Listing the asked-for claims would tell the user they're revealing a subset when they're revealing everything. That's the one misstatement a consent prompt must not make.

`discloses_whole_credentials()` states it explicitly, and a test pins it — so adding a selective-disclosure format (SD-JWT-VC, BBS+) fails that test and forces the prompt wording to be revisited alongside it.

## Also: the real cause of two Documentation CI failures

An outer `///` doc on a `pub mod X;` merges with that module's own `//!` docs and resolves in the **parent file's** scope — so every intra-doc link the module writes about its own items breaks. That's what failed CI on #192 and again here. #194 worked around the symptom by qualifying the link; that workaround is reverted, and the outer doc on `pub mod didcomm` is now a plain comment explaining why.

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed — 6 new tests
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

## Next

The wiring: a `credential-exchange/query` handler (messages already route in via the catch-all, but there's no handler, so a VTC challenge is currently dropped), the consent overlay, and `credential-exchange/present` on approval. Kept separate because this half is pure and unit-testable, and the wiring half is UI state.

title: feat: route trust tasks over TSP
body:
Closes **#185 item 2b**, unblocked by OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#803 / #810 — **vta-sdk 0.20.2 is published**.

## Why this was blocked, and what changed

TSP was unreachable from OpenVTC for a structural reason, not a missing feature. The only route to a Trust-Task-over-TSP client was `connect_tsp`, which opens its **own** websocket. The mediator permits one per DID and rejects the second with `duplicate-channel` — and the reference VTA points both `#tsp` and `#vta-didcomm` at the same mediator, so the collision was the *normal* case.

0.20.2 makes TSP a **per-surface leg of the existing DIDComm session**. `enable_tsp_trust_tasks` needs no second socket and performs no I/O: TSP send is an HTTP post to the mediator, and TSP receive already arrives on the pickup socket we hold, tagged by protocol. The API also refuses the duplicate-session case outright, so the defect I filed is unrepresentable through it.

## What moves — and what deliberately does not

| Surface | Transport |
|---|---|
| `dispatch_trust_task` — the six `did-management/agent-name` Trust Tasks | **TSP** |
| `get_key_secret`, `create_key`, `create_did_webvh`, `delete_did_webvh`, `list_contexts`, `list_webvh_servers` | **DIDComm, unconditionally** |

Those six have no TSP dispatcher behind them at the VTA. Moving them would break them — which is the whole reason TSP is a per-surface choice rather than a client-wide transport, and why the original framing in #185 (a third `VtaTransport` variant) was wrong.

## Best-effort by construction

Discovery is bounded at 5 s (R1.2), and **every** failure path — no `#tsp` advertised, resolve timeout, resolve error, or a split-mediator topology the API refuses — leaves the client exactly as `connect_auto` returned it: on DIDComm, fully working. TSP is an upgrade; it must never be able to fail a startup that would otherwise have succeeded.

`connect_auto` itself is unchanged in 0.20.2 (verified — no TSP arm), so the bump alters no existing transport selection.

## The panel

`TSP advertised (not yet supported)` → **`TSP for trust tasks`**.

Both the old text and a plain "also available" would now be wrong, in opposite directions: TSP is neither unusable nor an alternative to switch to. It carries part of the traffic while the rest stays on DIDComm, and that third state is what the panel has to express (R6.4). The test asserting the old wording is replaced by one asserting the new state and explicitly rejecting both wrong readings.

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean

title: feat: route trust tasks over TSP (#196)
body:
feat: route trust tasks over TSP (#196)

Closes #185 item 2b, unblocked by VTI #803 / #810 (vta-sdk 0.20.2).

TSP was previously unreachable from OpenVTC for a structural reason, not a
missing feature: the only route to a Trust-Task-over-TSP client was
connect_tsp, which opens its own websocket. The mediator permits one per
DID and rejects the second with duplicate-channel, and the reference VTA
points both #tsp and #vta-didcomm at the same mediator -- so the collision
was the normal case, not an edge one.

0.20.2 makes TSP a per-surface leg of the existing DIDComm session.
enable_tsp_trust_tasks needs no second socket and performs no I/O: TSP send
is an HTTP post to the mediator, and TSP receive already arrives on the
pickup socket we hold, tagged by protocol.

What moves, and what deliberately does not:

  * dispatch_trust_task and everything on it now routes over TSP -- for
    OpenVTC that is the six did-management/agent-name Trust Tasks.
  * rpc / rpc_void stay on DIDComm unconditionally. get_key_secret,
    create_key, create_did_webvh, delete_did_webvh, list_contexts and
    list_webvh_servers have no TSP dispatcher behind them at the VTA.
    Moving them would break them, which is the whole reason TSP is a
    per-surface choice rather than a client-wide transport.

Enabling it is best-effort by construction. Discovery is bounded at 5s
(R1.2) and every failure path -- no #tsp advertised, resolve timeout,
resolve error, or a split-mediator topology the API refuses -- leaves the
client exactly as connect_auto returned it, on DIDComm and fully working.
TSP is an upgrade; it must never be able to fail a startup that would
otherwise have succeeded.

The VTA panel stops saying 'TSP advertised (not yet supported)' and says
'TSP for trust tasks'. Both the old text and a plain 'also available' would
now be wrong, in opposite directions: TSP is neither unusable nor an
alternative transport to switch to. It carries part of the traffic while
the rest stays on DIDComm, and that third state is what the panel has to
express (R6.4).

Also boxed DegradedOutcome::Joined: VtaClient grew a TSP leg field, so the
variant now dwarfs Exit -- the common outcome -- and clippy flagged it.

Verified: all 16 test binaries pass with --include-ignored, clippy, fmt and
rustdoc -D warnings clean.

title: fix(sdk): TSP is a per-surface leg, not a whole-client transport (#803)
body:
Closes #803. Unblocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2b.

## The problem

A consumer holding a DIDComm session could not use TSP at all. The only route to a
Trust-Task-over-TSP client was `connect_tsp`, which opens its **own** websocket — and
the mediator permits one websocket per DID, so the second was rejected with
`duplicate-channel` and the two reconnect loops duelled. On the reference deployment
`#tsp` and `#vta-didcomm` resolve to the *same* mediator, so this was the normal case.

## What decided the design

**The VTA already fixed this on the server side.** `vta-service/src/server.rs:1056-1062`
deleted its standalone TSP websocket because it "made the mediator evict a connection as
`duplicate-channel`, flapping the VTA"; it now demuxes TSP off its single delivery-layer
socket. This PR is the client-side mirror of a fix already in production.

**The plumbing was already there and unused.** `DidCommTransport::inbound` polls
`live_stream_next_frame`, which yields **both** protocols off the one pickup socket and
tags each `Inbound` with `message.protocol`. TSP *send* is an HTTP `POST /inbound` — no
socket at all. So a full TSP leg on an existing DIDComm session costs **zero new sockets**.

## Changes

- **`DIDCommSession` TSP leg** — `send_tsp_document` / `request_tsp` / `receive_next_tsp`
  over the existing connection. The leg takes its own `subscribe()` receiver (subscribers
  are a broadcast), so the TSP pump cannot eat a DIDComm push and `receive_next` cannot eat
  a TSP reply.
- **`VtaClient::enable_tsp_trust_tasks`** — the seam #803 asks for. Moves the Trust-Task
  surface (`dispatch_trust_task`, `rpc_tt`, the `device/*` and `vault/*` methods) onto TSP.
  No I/O, cannot fail. `attach_tsp_leg` covers the split-mediator topology and **refuses**
  a second session for a DID on the mediator it is already connected to — the defect is
  unrepresentable through the API. `connect_didcomm_with_tsp` does both in one call.
- `rpc` / `rpc_void` stay on DIDComm unconditionally — the VTA has no TSP dispatcher behind
  `key-management/1.0/*`, `create_did_webvh` or `list_contexts`.
- **`SurfaceTransport` + `trust_task_transport()` / `protocol_message_transport()`** — a
  client no longer has *one* transport, so an operator display rendering a single value is
  wrong by construction (openvtc#185 item 2a).

### Live regression fixed on the pnm/cnm path

`TransportChoice::Auto` returned a **TSP-only** client whenever a VTA advertised `#tsp`,
so on a TSP-enabled VTA every protocol-message command (`keys create`, `contexts list`,
DID minting) failed with `UnsupportedTransport`. Auto now returns a **dual** client against
a VTA advertising both — one socket — and still falls back to TSP-only, loudly, when the
DIDComm mediator is down. Forced `--transport tsp` is unchanged (TSP-only by request).

### Also fixed

`DIDCommSession::receive_next` parsed every inbound frame as a DIDComm `Message`, so a TSP
frame on the multiplexed socket became a hard error on the DIDComm inbox that received it.
Latent on `main` only because nothing sent TSP to an SDK DIDComm session.

Reply correlation moved to a shared `tsp_demux` so `TspSession` and the new leg cannot
drift on the rule that stops a *stale* inbox frame being returned as a reply (#749). Its
parking queue is now bounded (previously unbounded).

## Verification

**Live, against the deployed VTA** (`glenn-vta`, both services on one mediator) — a trust
task dispatched over the DIDComm session's socket reached the VTA and its reply came back
correlated:

```
  TSP mediator:     did:webvh:QmTS3a…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
  DIDComm mediator: did:webvh:QmTS3a…:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
  ✅ TSP on the DIDComm session's socket: the VTA answered
  ✅ DIDComm (control): the VTA answered
```

`vta-sdk/tests/tsp_dual_leg_live.rs` (`#[ignore]`d, credential-free — a `permissionDenied`
trust-task *response* proves the transport; only a transport error fails it. Set
`VTA_LIVE_CLIENT_DID`/`_KEY` to tighten to a successful payload).

**Hermetic, in CI** — `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_dual_leg.rs` over the embedded `TestMediator`
(4 tests, all green): a TSP frame reaches a DID whose only connection is a `DIDCommSession`;
both legs work on that one session; `request_tsp` correlates its reply while an unrelated
push is parked, not eaten; and the API refuses the duplicate socket.

Plus unit coverage for the demux (correlation, nonce fallback, parking, concurrency,
bounded queue) and leg selection, `Send`-future assertions for the new call chain, `cargo
fmt`, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` clean.

`vta-sdk` 0.20.1 → 0.20.2 — additive only; a minor bump would break the workspace
`[patch.crates-io]` pin.

title: TSP: a consumer already holding a DIDComm session cannot use TSP — connect_tsp opens a second socket and the mediator rejects it (duplicate-channel)
body:
`vta-sdk` can construct a Trust-Task-over-TSP `VtaClient` only by opening its
**own** websocket. Any consumer that already holds a DIDComm session on the same
client DID therefore cannot use TSP at all: the mediator rejects the second
socket with `duplicate-channel`.

This blocks OpenVTC/openvtc#185 item 2b (route OpenVTC's trust-task surface over
TSP). Everything below is from trying to implement it.

**Verified against `origin/main` at cbfc3f83**, not just the published crate — the
in-tree `vta-sdk` is also `0.20.0`, `connect_tsp` still calls
`TspSession::connect`, `connect_auto` has no TSP arm, and there is no constructor
taking an existing session. So #797 (which closed #765/#766/#767) does not cover
this; it made TSP selectable for the session-store path, and this is the gap that
remains for every other consumer.

## The collision

`TspSession::connect` (`vta-sdk/src/session.rs:2233`) builds its own
`TDKSharedState`, its own `ATM`, its own `ATMProfile` for `client_did`, and calls
`atm.tsp().connect_websocket(&profile)`:

```rust
let atm = ATM::new(ATMConfig::builder().build()?, Arc::new(tdk)).await?;
let profile = ATMProfile::new(&atm, None, client_did.to_string(),
                              Some(mediator_did.to_string())).await?;
let ws = atm.tsp().connect_websocket(&profile).await?;
```

`VtaClient::connect_tsp` wraps that in `Transport::Tsp`, so there is no way to
obtain a TSP-capable `VtaClient` other than opening a fresh socket.

**The mediator permits one websocket per DID**, rejecting a second with
`duplicate-channel` — documented in `design-docs/vti-phase3-cutover-plan.md` §4
(investigated 2026-07-16), and restated in
`affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service/src/config.rs:14`:

> The mediator allows one websocket per DID, so a node speaking both protocols
> multiplexes them on the same socket rather than opening a second one.

A consumer holding a DIDComm session on `client_did` (the normal shape — the SDK's
own `LeakGuard` discipline is one `DIDCommSession` per `client_did`) cannot open a
`TspSession` on that same DID against that same mediator.

## It is the normal case, not an edge case

`Transport::Tsp`'s doc notes the TSP mediator is *"not assumed to equal the
DIDComm mediator"*, so a split-mediator deployment would dodge this. The
reference deployment does not split. Resolving
`did:webvh:QmWoJD2kpP6AJknNtj7UFERUstEen258ywj3ruHoh1ZAqr:webvh.storm.ws:glenn-vta`:

```
#tsp           TSPTransport      -> did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9Dk4ZMPAZ8jNWGeyPbuKrPbrPZcSbg8CJ6yynD:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
#vta-didcomm   DIDCommMessaging  -> did:webvh:QmTS3a3H9Dk4ZMPAZ8jNWGeyPbuKrPbrPZcSbg8CJ6yynD:webvh.storm.ws:mediator
```

Same mediator. So enabling TSP on a consumer that already speaks DIDComm produces
two sockets on one DID against one mediator.

Worth stating plainly: because the split-mediator topology *would* work, this is
the worst failure shape available — correct on an unusual deployment,
`duplicate-channel` plus duelling auto-reconnect loops on the reference one. That
is a diagnosis cost paid by whoever enables TSP next, and the symptom (a dropped
response on the first burst of requests) points nowhere near the cause.

## Why a consumer cannot work around it

- **Drop the DIDComm session while using TSP.** Not viable: TSP carries the
  Trust-Task surface only. `rpc`/`rpc_void` operations — `key-management/1.0/*`,
  `create_did_webvh`, `list_contexts`, `list_webvh_servers` — return
  `UnsupportedTransport` over TSP by design (`client/mod.rs:161`). A consumer needs
  both legs live simultaneously, which is exactly what the one-socket rule forbids
  across two sessions.
- **Use a different DID for the TSP session.** Changes the proven `sender_vid` the
  VTA authorizes against, so it is a different principal — not a workaround, a
  different security posture.
- **Reach TSP through the messaging layer instead.**
  `affinidi-messaging-didcomm-service` 0.3.20 already does the right thing:
  `Protocols::BOTH` multiplexes DIDComm + TSP on **one** socket, with a
  `TspHandler` symmetric to `DIDCommHandler`. But that socket is owned by
  `AffinidiMessageService`, and `VtaClient` has no constructor that accepts one —
  so a consumer can receive TSP frames there while still being unable to
  `dispatch_trust_task` over TSP.

That last point is the gap: the multiplexing already exists one layer down. What
is missing is the seam between it and `VtaClient`.

## Proposed direction

Either would unblock the consumer; (1) looks cheaper and composes with what
already exists.

1. **A `VtaClient` constructor over an existing multiplexed session** — e.g.
   `VtaClient::over_tsp_session(Arc<TspSession>, vta_did, mediator_did, rest_url)`,
   or accepting the messaging layer's socket, so the single multiplexed socket
   carries `dispatch_trust_task`. The consumer keeps one socket per DID and
   chooses per surface.

2. **`connect_auto` multiplexing both protocols itself** — one client, `rpc` on the
   DIDComm leg and `rpc_tt`/`dispatch_trust_task` on the TSP leg, with
   `Transport::Tsp`'s current all-or-nothing behaviour becoming the
   TSP-only-deployment case. This removes the per-surface decision from every
   consumer, at the cost of a larger change to `Transport`.

Whichever lands, the `TransportChoice` policy already written for
`SessionStore::connect_with_transport` (TSP > DIDComm > REST, bounded connects via
`TSP_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT`, deliberately loud fallback) should apply to it
rather than being re-derived — consumers not on the session-store path currently
cannot reach any of it.

## Notes

- Related: #765 / #766 / #767 (all closed) delivered discovery, `TransportChoice`,
  and the correlated request/response client. This is the remaining piece for a
  consumer that is not the `pnm`/`cnm` session-store path.
- Consumer-side context and the full investigation: OpenVTC/openvtc#185.
- Enabling the `tsp` feature itself is cheap: **+148,944 bytes, +0.82%** on the
  OpenVTC release binary (18,112,368 → 18,261,312; macOS arm64, `lto = true`,
  `strip = "symbols"`), building clean. Binary size is not what is holding this up.

title: refactor(vtc): admin passkeys move to the canonical auth/passkey tasks
body:
The VTI half of [trust-tasks-tf#145](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/145). Moves `/v1/admin/passkeys/*` off the retired `openvtc/vtc/` authority onto the canonical tasks that PR published (`trust-tasks-rs` 0.2.38 → 0.2.39).

**Three of the eight entries in `AWAITING_CANONICAL_FOLD` are gone.** #710 and #709 shrink accordingly; five remain.

## No wire change

The canonical specs were written **from this implementation**, not the other way round. Request and response bodies are byte-identical — only the `type` URIs moved.

## One task per ceremony leg, where there used to be one per family

`admin/passkeys/register/1.0` covered *both* `register/start` and `register/finish`; `revoke/1.0` likewise. A single schema spanning both legs has to permit the union of their members — which means **a `finish` arriving without its user-verification assertion still validated against the family task**. Each leg now names its own:

| Endpoint | Task |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/admin/passkeys` | `auth/passkey/list/0.1` |
| `POST …/register/start` | `auth/passkey/enroll/start/0.2` |
| `POST …/register/finish` | `auth/passkey/enroll/finish/0.2` |
| `POST …/revoke/start` | `auth/passkey/revoke/start/0.1` |
| `POST …/revoke/finish` | `auth/passkey/revoke/finish/0.1` |

## Every call site audited per leg, not renamed in bulk

A mount split means a bulk find-and-replace is exactly the wrong move — that's how splitting the VTC mounts earlier hid two admin-UI bugs. So all four binding sites were walked individually, each call site mapped to the endpoint it actually targets before being repointed:

- the router (5 mounts)
- `tests/admin_passkeys.rs` — **19 call sites**
- `tests/install_flow.rs` — 3
- `admin-ui/src/plugins/myPasskeys.tsx` — 4

The negative test that deliberately sends the wrong task to `register/start` still sends a wrong one.

## The recorded blocker was wrong

This is why these three sat unfolded so long. The note said each needed a **`confirm/1.0` gate**. Reading that spec: `confirm/request` is an **asynchronous** delegation whose response returns *out of band on the approver's own transport*. That is right when the approver is a separate party. It is wrong here — this surface verifies the user **in-band, in the same request**, via WebAuthn, and always did.

`enroll/*` moves to **0.2** because that is the version carrying the optional `uvOptions` / `uvCredential` members describing the re-authentication half this code already performs.

Worth noting for whoever picks up the rest: **`members/promote-to-admin` carries the same wrong blocker.** It is also a synchronous two-phase UV ceremony (`promote_start` / `promote_finish`). It is *not* a free fold though — its `finish` leg is fused, consuming the UV assertion *and* performing the role change, and `acl/change-role/0.1` requires `{subject, fromRole, toRole}` which the endpoint never carries. It needs either an API split or a new spec; both are judgement calls, not mechanical work.

## Retiring the superseded tasks

The manifest test refuses to publish a task no route binds, so `admin/passkeys/{list,register,revoke}/1.0` are marked `status: retired` + `supersededBy` in `trust-tasks/` and `index.json`, per SPEC §5.3 — the same treatment `admin/config/manage` got.

## Verification

- `cargo check --workspace --locked --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — full suite green
- `trust_task_manifest` 7/7 · `admin_passkeys` 12/12 · `install_flow` 1/1
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — no warnings
- `cargo fmt --check`, version-bump guard, changelog guard, lockfile self-pin guard — all pass

Refs #710, #709.

title: feat: rebuild a listener whose ATM has died
body:
Closes the gap I named in #194 rather than filled at the time.

## What was missing

`DidCommTransport::inbound()` survives a socket drop — the ATM reconnects underneath it — so ordinary churn needs no supervision. What it cannot survive is **the ATM task itself dying**: the transport is then permanently `Disconnected` with nothing retrying behind it, and the listener is stranded until the process restarts. The framework's `RestartPolicy` used to cover that; the delivery layer has no equivalent.

## The hard part is not rebuilding — it's not rebuilding too eagerly

`ConnState::Disconnected` means *"dropped, retrying or idle"*, not *"gone"*. A supervisor that reacted to it would open a second websocket for a DID whose ATM is already retrying, and the mediator rejects the second with `duplicate-channel` — **manufacturing the duelling-reconnect fault the supervisor exists to recover from** (#132).

So the grace period being generous *is* the safety property, not conservatism:

- **`REBUILD_GRACE` (90 s)** must exceed the window a healthy reconnect needs. A test asserts it also exceeds the backoff ceiling, so a rebuild can never be scheduled sooner than a normal recovery would have finished.
- **Backoff 5 s → 10 s → 20 s → 40 s, capped at 60 s** — the framework's old policy, including `max_retries: None`. A mediator that returns hours later is picked up without restarting the app.
- **Remove before add**, for the same one-socket-per-DID reason.
- A listener removed *deliberately* (community left, DID deleted) between the state sample and the rebuild is dropped from tracking, not resurrected.

`IdentityWire` now retains its `ListenerSpec`, since rebuilding means constructing a fresh ATM, profile and transport from the same inputs.

## Why the policy is two pure functions

`rebuild_due` and `rebuild_backoff` are split out of the loop because that is where the entire risk lives — too eager causes `duplicate-channel`, never causes a stranded listener — and a pure function is something tests can pin in **both** directions. Six unit tests do, including that a drop one second old is left alone, and that a day-long outage still retries.

The integration test earns its keep separately: over a real mediator, across several supervisor ticks, a connected listener reports no disconnect transition and stays `Connected`. **A supervisor that rebuilt on every tick would pass every unit test and fail this one.**

## Verification

- All **16** test binaries pass with `--include-ignored`, 0 failed
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — clean
- `cargo fmt --all --check` — clean
- `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` — clean

## Still not covered, and I'd rather say so

No test kills an ATM and observes a real rebuild — I could not find a way to tear one down from outside the SDK without reaching into its internals. So the *trigger* is verified by construction and by the policy tests; the *rebuild path itself* shares its code with `add_listener`, which the other e2e tests exercise. If you know a way to kill an ATM cleanly in the test mediator, that would close the last of it.

title: feat: rebuild a listener whose ATM has died (#195)
body:
feat: rebuild a listener whose ATM has died (#195)

Closes the gap named in #194. The delivery-layer swap left one thing the
framework used to do uncovered: nothing rebuilt a transport whose ATM task
had died.

DidCommTransport::inbound() survives a socket drop -- the ATM reconnects
underneath it -- so ordinary churn needs no supervision. What it cannot
survive is the ATM task itself dying: the transport is then permanently
Disconnected with nothing retrying behind it, and the listener is stranded
until the process restarts. The framework's RestartPolicy covered that.

The hard part is not the rebuild, it is not doing it too eagerly.
ConnState::Disconnected means "dropped, retrying or idle", not "gone". A
supervisor that reacted to it would open a second websocket for a DID
whose ATM is already retrying, and the mediator rejects the second with
duplicate-channel -- manufacturing the duelling-reconnect fault the
supervisor exists to recover from (#132).

So the grace period being generous IS the safety property:

  * REBUILD_GRACE (90s) must exceed the window a healthy reconnect needs.
    A test asserts it also exceeds the backoff ceiling, so a rebuild can
    never be scheduled sooner than a normal recovery would have finished.
  * Consecutive failures back off 5s/10s/20s/40s, capped at 60s -- the
    framework's old policy, including max_retries: None. A mediator that
    comes back hours later is picked up without restarting the app.
  * A rebuild removes before it adds, for the same one-socket-per-DID
    reason.
  * A listener removed deliberately (community left, DID deleted) between
    the state sample and the rebuild is dropped from tracking, not
    resurrected.

IdentityWire now retains its ListenerSpec, since rebuilding means
constructing a fresh ATM, profile and transport from the same inputs.

The decision is split into two pure functions (rebuild_due,
rebuild_backoff) because that is where the whole risk lives -- too eager
causes duplicate-channel, never causes a stranded listener -- and pure
functions are what tests can pin in both directions. Six unit tests do,
including that a drop one second old is left alone and that a day-long
outage still retries.

One integration test over a real mediator asserts the loop honours those
thresholds in practice: across several supervisor ticks a connected
listener reports no disconnect transition and stays Connected. That is
the failure mode worth catching, since a supervisor that rebuilt every
tick would still pass every unit test.

and rustdoc -D warnings clean.

title: fix(specs): relative links resolve, and a guard so they keep resolving
body:
136 broken relative links across 65 `spec.md` files — plus the check that should have caught them.

## What was wrong

Relative links in spec prose resolve from the **version** directory (`specs/<slug>/<version>/`), because that is where `spec.md` lives and where it is served from — `build-registry.mjs` syncs `specs/` verbatim to `website/specs/<slug>/<version>/`.

135 of the 136 were written as though they resolved from the **slug** directory, one level shallower. From `auth/passkey/enroll/start/0.1`, `../finish/0.1/spec.md` points at `.../start/finish/0.1/`, which has never existed.

**These were broken on the live site, not merely in the repo.**

The single outlier was not a depth error at all: `vtc/policies/test` linked to `vtc/policies/upload`, which does not exist under *any* depth. That task was repointed onto the canonical `policy/upsert/0.2` (VTI #729) and the link never followed. Retargeted rather than mechanically deepened.

`bindings/` was already clean and is unchanged.

## The guard is the point

A sweep without one regresses immediately — 135 links drifted the same way precisely because nothing checked. `build-registry.mjs` now resolves every relative markdown link and fails the build on a miss. When the target resolves one level deeper, it says so, because that is the mistake people will actually make:

```
auth/passkey/list/0.1/spec.md: relative link '../revoke/start/0.1/spec.md' does not
resolve — one level too shallow; '../../revoke/start/0.1/spec.md' resolves
```

Verified **both** directions: a clean build across all 246 specs, and a deliberately reintroduced break failing with exactly the message above.

## No version bump

Codegen drift is **zero** — the bindings generate from `payload.schema.json`, and this touches only prose and the build script. Confirmed with `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`: no diff under `trust-tasks-rs/src` or `trust-tasks-ts/src`.
